passages.original: Nempe aput Vergilium, quem propterea paruuli legunt, ut uidelicet poeta magnus omniumque praeclarissimus adque optimus teneris ebibitus animis non facile obliuione possit aboleri, secundum illud Horatii: Quo semel est inbuta recens sernabit odorem Testa diu - aput hunc ergo Vergilium nempe Iuno inducitur infesta Troianis Aeolo uentorum regi aduersus eos inritando dicere: Gens inimica mihi Tyrrhenum nauigat aequor Ilium in Italiam portans uictosque penates.
passages.english: Indeed, in Virgil, whom little boys read precisely so that this great poet, the most illustrious and best of all, drunk in by tender minds, may not easily be blotted out by forgetfulness, according to that saying of Horace: "The jar will long keep the scent with which it was once steeped when new" — in this Virgil, then, Juno is indeed brought on, hostile to the Trojans, saying to Aeolus, king of the winds, as she stirs him up against them: "A race hateful to me sails the Tyrrhenian sea, carrying Ilium and its conquered household gods into Italy."
passages.notes: "sernabit" read as "seruabit" (scanning error).

passages.original: Quid Aeneas ipse, pius totiens appellatus, nonne ita narrat: Panthus Othryades, arcis Phoebique sacerdos, Sacra manu uictosque deos paruumque nepotem Ipse trahit cursuque amens ad limina tendit? Nonne deos ipsos, quos uictos non dubitat dicere, sibi potius quam se illis perhibet commendatos, cum ei dicitur: Sacra suosqne tibi commendat Troia penates? Si igitur Vergilius tales deos et uictos dicit et, ut uel uicti quoquo modo euaderent, homini commendatos: quae dementia est existimare his tutoribus Romam sapienter fuisse commissam et nisi eos amisisset non potuisse uastari? Immo uero uictos deos tamquam praesides ac defensores colere, quid est aliud quam tenere non numina bona, sed nomina mala?
passages.english: What of Aeneas himself, so often called dutiful? Does he not tell it thus: "Panthus, son of Othrys, priest of the citadel and of Phoebus, himself drags along in his hand the sacred objects, the conquered gods, and his little grandson, and, out of his mind, heads at a run for the threshold"? Does he not declare that the very gods whom he does not hesitate to call conquered were entrusted to him rather than he to them, when it is said to him: "Troy entrusts to you her sacred things and her household gods"? If, then, Virgil calls such gods both conquered and, so that even when conquered they might escape somehow, entrusted to a man, what madness is it to think that Rome was wisely committed to these guardians, and that it could not have been laid waste unless it had lost them? Rather, to worship conquered gods as protectors and defenders, what is that but to hold not good divinities but bad omens?
passages.notes: Wordplay "non numina bona, sed nomina mala" (not good powers but evil names/omens) cannot be reproduced in English. "suosqne" read as "suosque".

passages.original: Quem morem etiam Cato, sicut scribit Sallustius, nobilitatae ueritatis historicus, sententia sua, quam de coniuratis in senatu habuit, conmemorare non praetermittit: \'rapi uirgines pueros, diuelli liberos a parentum conplexu, matres familiarum pati quae uictoribus conlibuisset, fana adque domos spoliari, caedem incendia fieri: postremo armis cadaueribus cruore adque luctu omnia conpleri\'. Hic si fana tacuisset, deorum sedibus solere hostes parcere putaremus.
passages.english: This custom Cato too, as Sallust, a historian of renowned truthfulness, writes, does not fail to mention in the speech he delivered in the senate concerning the conspirators: "that maidens and boys are carried off, children torn from their parents' embrace, mothers of families made to suffer whatever the victors please, shrines and houses plundered, slaughter and burning carried out; in short, everything filled with arms, corpses, blood and mourning." If he had kept silent here about shrines, we would suppose that enemies were accustomed to spare the dwellings of the gods.

passages.original: sed demonstrentur uel commemorentur loca talibus aliquando conuenticulis consecrata, non ubi ludi agerentur obscenis uocibus et motibus histrionum, nec ubi Fugalia celebrantur effusa omni licentia turpitudinum (et uere Fugalia, sed pudoris et honestatis); sed ubi populi audirent quid di praeciperent de cohibenda auaritia, ambitione frangenda, luxuria refrenanda, ubi discerent miseri, quod discendum Persius increpat dicens: Discite, o miseri, et causas cognoscite rerum, Quid sumus et quidnam uicturi gignimur, ordo Quis datus aut metae qua mollis flexus et unde, Quis modus argenti, quid fas optare, quid asper Utile nummus habet, patriae carisque propinquis Quantum largiri deceat, quem te Deus esse Iussit et humana qua parte locatus es in re. Dicatur in quibus locis haec docentium deorum solebant praecepta recitari et a cultoribus eorum populis frequenter audiri, sicut nos ostendimus ad hoc ecclesias institutas, quaqua uersum religio Christiana diffunditur.
passages.english: but let them point out or name places at some time consecrated to such gatherings — not where games were performed with the obscene words and gestures of actors, nor where the Fugalia are celebrated with every licence for indecency let loose (truly a Fugalia, a flight, but of modesty and decency); but where the peoples might hear what the gods commanded about restraining avarice, breaking ambition, curbing luxury; where the wretched might learn what Persius, rebuking them, says must be learned: "Learn, you wretched ones, and come to know the causes of things: what we are, and for what life we are born, what rank is given us, or where the gentle turn around the turning-post is and from where, what limit there is to money, what it is right to wish for, what use hard coin has, how much it is fitting to bestow on one's country and dear kinsmen, what God has commanded you to be, and in what part of the human order you have been placed." Let it be said in what places these precepts of teaching gods used to be recited and frequently heard by the peoples who worshipped them, just as we show that churches have been established for this purpose wherever the Christian religion spreads.
passages.notes: Fugalia: an obscure Roman festival; Augustine puns on fuga, "flight".

passages.original: Quanto satius erat ad erudiendam iustitia iuuentutem publice recitari leges deorum quam laudari inaniter leges adque instituta maiorum! Omnes enim cultores talium deorum, mox ut eos libido perpulerit feruenti, ut ait Persius, tincta ueneno, magis intuentur quid Iuppiter fecerit, quam quid docuerit Plato uel censuerit Cato. Hinc aput Terentium flagitiosus adulescens spectat tabulam quandam pictam in pariete,ubi inerat pictura haec, Iouem Quo pacto Danaae misisse aiunt quondam in gremium imbrem aureum, adque ab hac tanta auctoritate adhibet patrocinium turpitudini suae, cum in ea se iactat imitari deum.
passages.english: How much better it would have been, for instructing the young in justice, that the laws of the gods be recited publicly than that the laws and institutions of the ancestors be praised in vain! For all the worshippers of such gods, as soon as lust has driven them on, "dipped in burning poison," as Persius says, look rather to what Jupiter did than to what Plato taught or Cato judged. Hence in Terence a profligate youth looks at a painted panel on a wall, "in which there was this picture: how Jupiter, they say, once sent a golden shower into Danaë's lap," and from this great authority he borrows a defence for his own vileness, when he boasts that in it he is imitating a god.

passages.original: Quid hinc autem senserint Romani ueteres, Cicero testatur in libris, quos de re publica scripsit, ubi Scipio disputans ait: \'Numquam comoediae, nisi consuetudo uitae pateretur, probare sua theatris flagitia potuissent\'. Et Graeci quidem antiquiores uitiosae suae opinionis quandam conuenientiam seruarunt, aput quos fuit etiam lege concessum, ut quod uellet comoedia, de quo uellet, nominatim diceret. Itaque, sicut in eisdem libris loquitur Africanus, quem illa non adtigit, uel potius quem non uexauit?
passages.english: What the ancient Romans thought about this, Cicero testifies in the books he wrote On the Republic, where Scipio, in the discussion, says: "Comedies could never have made their outrages acceptable in the theatres, unless the custom of life had allowed it." And the older Greeks at least kept a certain consistency with their faulty opinion, since among them it was even granted by law that comedy might say what it wished, about whom it wished, by name. And so, as Africanus says in the same books, whom did it not touch, or rather whom did it not harass?

passages.original: Patiamur, inquit, etsi eius modi ciues a censore melius est quam a poeta notari. Sed Periclen, cum iam suae ciuitati maxima auctoritate plurimos annos domi et belli praefuisset, uiolari uersibus et eos agi in scaena non plus decuit, quam si Plautus, inquit, noster uoluisset aut Naeuius Publio et Gn. Scipioni aut Caecilius Marco Catoni maledicere.\' Dein paulo post: \'Nostrae, inquit, contra duodecim tabulae cum perpaucas res capite sanxissent, in his hanc quoque sanciendam putauerunt, si quis occentauisset siue carmen condidisset, quod infamiam faceret flagitiumue alteri.
passages.english: 'Let us put up with it,' he says, 'although citizens of that kind are better branded by a censor than by a poet. But for Pericles, when he had already presided over his city with the greatest authority for very many years in peace and in war, to be abused in verse and for those [verses] to be performed on the stage was no more fitting than if our Plautus,' he says, 'or Naevius had wished to slander Publius and Gnaeus Scipio, or Caecilius Marcus Cato.' Then a little later: 'Our Twelve Tables, on the other hand,' he says, 'though they made very few things capital offences, thought that this too should be included among them: if anyone had chanted abuse or composed a song that brought disgrace or dishonour on another.
passages.notes: Augustine is quoting Cicero, De re publica book 4, as the following context makes clear; the speaker here is Scipio Africanus.

passages.original: Itane pluris tibi habenda est existimatio curiae uestrae quam Capitolii, immo Romae unius quam caeli totius, ut linguam maledicam in ciues tuos exercere poetae etiam lege prohiberentur, et in deos tuos securi tanta conuicia nullo senatore nullo censore, nullo principe nullo pontifice prohibente iacularentur? Indignum uidelicet fuit, ut Plautus aut Naeuius [Publio et] Gn. Scipioni aut Caecilius M. Catoni malediceret, et dignum fuit, ut Terentius uester flagitio Iouis optimi maximi adulescentium nequitiam concitaret?
passages.english: Is the reputation of your senate-house, then, to be valued more by you than that of the Capitol, indeed of Rome alone more than of the whole heaven, so that poets were forbidden even by law to exercise an abusive tongue against your citizens, while against your gods they hurled such great insults without fear, with no senator, no censor, no emperor, no pontiff forbidding it? It was unworthy, of course, for Plautus or Naevius to slander [Publius and] Gnaeus Scipio, or Caecilius Marcus Cato; and was it worthy that your Terence should stir up the wickedness of young men through the outrage of Jupiter Best and Greatest?
passages.notes: "[Publio et]" is an editorial supplement.

passages.original: Itemque Romani, quamuis iam superstitione noxia premerentur, ut illos deos colerent, quos uidebant sibi uoluisse scaenicas turpitudines consecrari, suae tamen dignitatis memores ac pudoris actores talium fabularum nequaquam honorauerunt more Graecorum, sed, sicut aput Ciceronem idem Scipio loquitur, \'cum artem ludicram scaenamque totam in probro ducerent, genus id hominum non modo honore ciuium reliquorum carere, sed etiam tribu moueri notatione censoria uoluerunt.\' Praeclara sane et Romanis laudibus adnumeranda prudentia; sed uellem se ipsa sequeretur, se imitaretur. Ecce enim recte, quisquis ciuium Romanorum esse scaenicus elegisset, non solum ei nullus ad honorem dabatur locus, uerum etiam censoris nota tribum tenere propriam minime sinebatur.s o animum ciuitatis laudis auidum germaneque Romanum!
passages.english: Likewise the Romans, although already oppressed by a harmful superstition so as to worship those gods whom they saw had wished stage indecencies to be consecrated to them, yet, mindful of their own dignity and modesty, by no means honoured the actors of such plays, as the Greeks did; but, as the same Scipio says in Cicero, "since they held the art of acting and the whole stage as a disgrace, they wished that class of men not only to be deprived of the honours of other citizens but also to be removed from their tribe by the censor's mark." An excellent prudence indeed, and one to be counted among Roman glories; but I could wish it followed itself, imitated itself. For see: rightly, whoever of Roman citizens chose to be an actor not only was given no place for office, but was by no means allowed, through the censor's mark, to keep his own tribe. O spirit of a city eager for praise and truly Roman!
passages.notes: ".s o" read as "O" (scanning error).

passages.original: An forte populo Romano propterea leges non sunt a numinibus constitutae, quia, sicut Sallustius ait, \'ius bonumque aput eos non legibus magis quam natura ualebat\'? Ex hoc iure ac bono credo raptas Sabinas. Quid enim iustius et melius quam filias alienas fraude spectaculi inductas non a parentibus accipi, sed ui, ut quisque poterat, auferri? Nam si inique facerent Sabini negare postulatas, quanto fuit iniquius rapere non datas?
passages.english: Or perhaps laws were not established for the Roman people by the divinities because, as Sallust says, "right and good prevailed among them not by laws more than by nature"? By this right and good, I suppose, the Sabine women were carried off. For what is more just and better than that other men's daughters, lured by the trickery of a spectacle, should not be received from their parents but taken by force, as each man could? For if the Sabines acted unjustly in refusing them when asked, how much more unjust was it to seize them when not given?

passages.original: Nam cum optimis moribus et maxima concordia populum Romanum inter secundum et postremum bellum Carthaginiense commemorasset egisse causamque huius boni non amorem iustitiae, sed stante Carthagine metum pacis infidae fuisse dixisset (unde et Nasica ille ad reprimendam nequitiam seruandosque istos mores optimos, ut metu uitia cohiberentur, Carthaginem nolebat euerti): continuo subiecit idem Sallustius et ait: (At discordia et auaritia adque ambitio et cetera secundis rebus oriri sueta mala post Carthaginis excidium maxime aucta sunt\', ut intellegeremus etiam ante oriri solere et augeri: Unde subnectens quur hoc dixerit: *Nam iniuriae, inquit, ualidiorum et ob eas discessio plebis a patribus aliaeque dissensiones domi fuere iam inde a principio, neque amplius quam regibus exactis, dum metus a Tarquinio et bellum graue cum Etruria positum est, aequo et modesto iure agitatum.\' Vides quem ad modum etiam illo breui tempore, ut regibus exactis, id est eiectis, aliquantum aequo et modesto iure ageretur, metum dixit fuisse causam, quoniam metuebatur bellum, quod rex Tarquinius regno adque Urbe pulsus Etruscis sociatus contra Romanos gerebat.
passages.english: For when he had recorded that the Roman people lived with the best morals and the greatest concord between the second and the last Carthaginian war, and had said that the cause of this good was not love of justice but, while Carthage stood, fear of an untrustworthy peace (which is why the famous Nasica did not want Carthage destroyed, so as to repress wickedness and preserve those best morals, that vices might be restrained by fear), the same Sallust immediately added: "But discord and avarice and ambition and the other evils that usually arise in prosperity increased greatly after the destruction of Carthage," so that we should understand that they used to arise and grow even before. Then, adding why he said this: "For the wrongs done by the more powerful, and the consequent secession of the plebs from the patricians, and other dissensions at home existed from the very beginning; nor were affairs conducted with fair and moderate law any longer than, after the kings were driven out, until fear of Tarquin and the heavy war with Etruria were laid aside." You see how even for that short time, when after the kings were driven out, that is, expelled, affairs were conducted with fairly fair and moderate law, he said fear was the cause, since the war was feared which King Tarquin, driven from his kingdom and the City and allied with the Etruscans, was waging against the Romans.
passages.notes: "dum ... positum est" is usually understood as "until fear of Tarquin and the heavy war with Etruria were laid aside"; Augustine's own gloss implies "while the fear lasted", but the translation follows the usual sense.

passages.original: (Ex quo tempore, ut ait, maiorum mores non paulatim ut antea, sed torrentis modo praecipitati, adeo iuuentus luxu adque auaritia corrupta, ut merito dicatur genitos esse, qui neque ipsi habere possent res familiares neque alios pati.\' Dicit deinde plura Sallustius de Syllae uitiis ceteraque foeditate rei publicae, et alii scriptores in haec consentiunt, quamuis eloquio multum inpari.
passages.english: ("From that time," as he says, "the customs of the ancestors were hurled headlong, not gradually as before, but like a torrent; the youth were so corrupted by luxury and avarice that it may rightly be said that men were born who could neither keep property of their own nor allow others to keep theirs.") Sallust then says much more about the vices of Sulla and the other foulness of the republic, and other writers agree on these things, though far unequal in eloquence.

passages.original: Quando ergo res publica Romana talis erat, qualem illam describit Sallustius, non iam pessima ac flagitiosissima, sicut ipse ait, sed omnino nulla erat secundum istam rationem, quam disputatio de re publica inter magnos eius tum principes habita patefecit. Sicut etiam ipse Tullius non Scipionis nec cuiusquam alterius, sed suo sermone loquens in principio quinti libri commemorato prius Ennii poetae uersu, quo dixerat:. Moribus antiquis res stat Romana uirisque, \'quem quidem ille uersum, inquit, uel breuitate uel ueritate tamquam ex oraculo quodam mihi [ esse] effatus uidetur. Nam neque uiri, nisi ita morata ciuitas fuisset, neque mores. nisi hi uiri praefuissent, aut fundare aut tam diu tenere potuissent tantam et tam iuste longe lateque imperantem rem publicam.
passages.english: When, therefore, the Roman republic was such as Sallust describes it, it was no longer "the worst and most shameful," as he himself says, but was no republic at all, according to that reasoning which the discussion about the republic held among its great leading men of that time made clear. So too Tullius himself, speaking not in the person of Scipio or of anyone else but in his own words, at the beginning of the fifth book, after first quoting the verse of the poet Ennius in which he had said: "The Roman state stands on its ancient customs and its men," says: "This verse, for its brevity and its truth alike, seems to me to have been uttered as if from some oracle. For neither the men, unless the citizen body had been of such character, nor the customs, unless these men had been in charge, could have either founded or held for so long a republic so great and ruling so justly far and wide."
passages.notes: The bracketed [esse] is the edition's; it does not affect the sense.

passages.original: Sylla certe ipse, cuius tempora talia fuerunt, ut superiora, quorum uindex esse uidebatur, illorum conparatione quaererentur, cum primum ad Urbem contra Marium castra mouisset, adeo laeta exta immolanti fuisse scribit Liuius, ut custodiri se Postumius haruspex uoluerit capitis supplicium subiturus, nisi ea, quae in animo Sylla haberet, dis iuuantibus inpleuisset. Ecce non discesserant adytis adquo aris relictis di, quando de rerum euentu praedicebant nihilque de ipsius Syllae correctione curabant.
passages.english: Sulla himself, certainly, whose times were such that the earlier times, of which he seemed to be the avenger, were missed by comparison with them — when he first moved his camp against Marius toward the City, Livy writes that the entrails were so favourable when he sacrificed that the haruspex Postumius wished to be held in custody, ready to undergo capital punishment if Sulla did not, with the gods' help, accomplish what he had in mind. See, the gods had not "departed, leaving their shrines and altars," when they were foretelling the outcome of events and cared nothing about the correction of Sulla himself.
passages.notes: "adquo" read as "adque" (atque). The quoted phrase is from Virgil, Aeneid 2.

passages.original: Vir grauis et philosophaster Tullius aedilis futurus clamat in auribus ciuitatis, inter cetera sui magistratus officia sibi Floram matrem ludorum celebritate placandam; qui ludi tanto deuotius, quanto turpius celebrari solent. Dicit alio loco iam consul in extremis periculis ciuitatis, et ludos per decem dies factos, neque rem ullam quae ad placandos deos pertineret praetermissam;
passages.english: Tullius, a grave man and a would-be philosopher, when about to be aedile, cries out in the hearing of the city that among the other duties of his magistracy he must appease Mother Flora with the celebration of games; and these games are usually celebrated the more devoutly, the more obscenely. In another place, when already consul, in the extreme dangers of the city, he says that games had been held for ten days and that nothing which pertained to appeasing the gods had been omitted;

passages.original: Non ergo Ilium etiam tunc, ab eis cum desereretur, euersum est. Nam daemones ad decipiendum semper uigilantissimi, quod potuerunt, fecerunt. Euersis quippe et incensis omnibus cum oppido simulacris solum Mineruae sub tanta ruina templi illius, ut scribit Liuius, integrum stetisse perhibetur, non ut [diceretur] Di patrii, quorum semper sub numine Troia est, ad eorum laudem, sed ne diceretur: Excessere omnes adytis arisque relictis Di, ad eorum defensionem.
passages.english: So Ilium was not overthrown even then, when it was abandoned by them. For the demons, always most watchful to deceive, did what they could. When all the images had been overthrown and burned together with the town, only that of Minerva, as Livy writes, is said to have stood intact beneath the great ruin of her temple — not so that it might be said, to their praise, "Ancestral gods, under whose divine power Troy always stands," but so that it might not be said, in their defence, "All the gods have departed, leaving their shrines and altars."
passages.notes: Both quotations are from Virgil, Aeneid 9 and 2. The bracketed [diceretur] is supplied by the edition.

passages.original: Nunc autem non ei di contulerunt illud otium, sed eum minus fortasse decepissent, si otiosum minime repperissent. Quanto enim minus eum occupatum inuenerunt, tanto magis ipsi occupauerunt. Nam quid ille molitus sit et quibus artibus deos tales sibi uel illi ciuitati consociare potuerit, Varro prodit, quod, si Domino placuerit, suo diligentius disseretur loco. Modo autem quia de beneficiis eorum quaestio est: magnum beneficium est pax, sed Dei ueri beneficium est, plerumque etiam sicut sol, sicut pluuia uitaeque alia subsidia super ingratos et nequam.
passages.english: As it is, however, those gods did not bestow that leisure on him; rather, they would perhaps have deceived him less if they had not found him at leisure at all. For the less occupied they found him, the more they themselves occupied him. For what he contrived, and by what arts he was able to associate such gods with himself or with that city, Varro relates; this, if it pleases the Lord, will be discussed more carefully in its proper place. For now, since the question concerns their benefits: peace is a great benefit, but it is a benefit of the true God, often given, like the sun, like the rain and the other supports of life, even to the ungrateful and the wicked.

passages.original: Nonne in corporibus hominum satius est modicam staturam cum sanitate habere quam ad molem aliquam giganteam perpetuis adflictionibus peruenire, nec cum perueneris requiescere, sed quanto grandioribus membris, tanto maioribus agitari malis? Quid autem mali esset, ac non potius plurimum boni, si ea tempora perdurarent, quae perstrinxit Sallustius, ubi ait: \'Igitur initio reges (nam in terris nomen imperii id primum fuit) diuersi pars ingenium, alii corpus exercebant; etiamtum uita hominum sine cupiditate agitabatur, sua cuique satis placebant\'. An ut tam multum augeretur imperium, debuit fieri quod Vergilius detestatur, dicens: Deterior donec paulatim et decolor aetas Et belli rabies et amor successit habendi? Sed plane pro tantis bellis susceptis et gestis iusta defensio Romanorum est, quod inruentibus sibi inportune inimicis resistere cogebat non auiditas adipiscendae laudis humanae, sed necessitas tuendae salutis et libertatis.
passages.english: In human bodies, is it not better to have a moderate stature with health than to arrive at some gigantic bulk through constant afflictions, and when you have arrived, not to rest, but to be tossed by greater evils the larger the limbs? And what evil would there be, or rather would there not be very much good, if those times had lasted which Sallust touched on, where he says: "In the beginning, then, kings (for that was the first name of rule on earth) were of different minds: some exercised the intellect, others the body; at that time the life of men was still passed without greed; each was content with his own"? Or, in order that the empire might be so greatly increased, did there have to come about what Virgil abhors, saying: "Until little by little a worse and discoloured age / and the madness of war and the love of possessing took its place"? But plainly, for such great wars undertaken and waged, the Romans have a just defence: that what compelled them to resist enemies rushing upon them unprovoked was not greed for gaining human praise but the necessity of protecting their safety and freedom.

passages.original: sed undecumque nata sit, non, opinor, audebunt eam dicere ignobilem di peregrini deam ciuem Romanam. Sub hoc tot deorum praesidio (quos numerare quis potest, indigenas et alienigenas, caelites terrestres infernos, marinos fontanos fluuiales, et, ut Varro dicit, certos adque incertos, in omnibusque generibus deorum, sicut in animalibus, mares et feminas?) — sub hoc ergo tot deorum praesidio constituta Roma non tam magnis et horrendis cladibus, quales ex multis paucas commemorabo, agitari adfligique debuit.
passages.english: but from wherever she was born, the foreign gods will not, I think, dare to call her, a Roman citizen goddess, ignoble. Placed under the protection of so many gods (and who can count them, native and foreign, heavenly, earthly, infernal, of the sea, of springs, of rivers, and, as Varro says, 'certain' and 'uncertain', and in every kind of god, as among animals, males and females?), placed, then, under the protection of so many gods, Rome ought not to have been shaken and afflicted by such great and horrible disasters as those, a few out of many, that I shall recount.
passages.notes: The opening clause continues a sentence begun in the preceding passage (about the goddess Fever); its construction is somewhat awkward.

passages.original: nam et alii scriptores eorum defectioni solis addunt etiam subitam tempestatem, quae profecto aut occasionem sceleri praebuit aut Romulum ipsa consumsit.) De Tullo quippe etiam Hostilio, qui tertius a Romulo rex fuit, quia et ipse fulmine absumtus est, dicit in eisdem libris idem Cicero, propterea et istum non creditum in deos receptum tali morte, quia fortasse quod erat in Romulo probatum, id est persuasum, Romani uulgare noluerunt, id est uile facere, si hoc et alteri facile tribueretur.
passages.english: for other writers too add to the eclipse of the sun a sudden storm as well, which surely either provided the occasion for the crime or itself carried Romulus off.) Indeed, concerning Tullus Hostilius also, who was the third king after Romulus, since he too was destroyed by lightning, the same Cicero says in the same books that he was not believed to have been received among the gods by such a death for this reason: perhaps the Romans did not wish to make common — that is, to cheapen — what had been approved, that is, believed, in the case of Romulus, if it were readily attributed to another as well.

passages.original: Huic tempori adiciamus etiam tempus illud, quo usque dicit Sallustius aequo et modesto iure agitatum, dum metus a Tarquinio et bellum graue cum Etruria positum est. Quamdiu enim Etrusci Tarquinio in regnum redire conanti opitulati sunt, graui bello Roma concussa est.
passages.english: To this period let us add also that period up to which Sallust says affairs were conducted with fair and moderate justice, until the fear of Tarquin and the heavy war with Etruria were laid to rest. For as long as the Etruscans helped Tarquin in his attempt to return to the throne, Rome was shaken by a heavy war.

passages.original: hiems illa memorabilis tam incredibili inmanitate saeuiens, ut niuibus horrenda altitudine etiam in foro per dies quadraginta manentibus Tiberis quoque glacie , duraretur, si nostris temporibus accidisset, quae isti et quanta dixissent! Quid? illa itidem ingens pestilentia, quamdiu saeuiit, quam multos peremit! Quae cum in annum alium multo grauius tenderetur frustra praesente Aesculapio, aditum est ad libros Sibyllinos. In quo genere oraculorum, sicut Cicero in libris de diuinatione commemorat, magis interpretibus ut possunt seu uolunt dubia coniectantibus credi solet. Tunc ergo dictum est eam esse causam pestilentiae, quod plurimas aedes sacras multi occupatas priuatim tenerent: sic interim a magno inperitiae uel desidiae crimine Aesculapius liberatus est.
passages.english: That memorable winter, raging with such incredible severity that, with snow of dreadful depth lying even in the Forum for forty days, the Tiber too was frozen hard with ice — if it had happened in our times, what things and how many would these people have said! What then? That likewise huge pestilence, as long as it raged, how many it killed! When it extended into another year much more severely, Aesculapius being present in vain, recourse was had to the Sibylline books. In this kind of oracle, as Cicero recalls in his books On Divination, it is usual to believe rather the interpreters, who make conjectures about doubtful matters as they can or as they wish. Then, therefore, it was said that the cause of the pestilence was that many people were holding very many sacred buildings that they had occupied for private use; thus for the moment Aesculapius was freed from the great charge of incompetence or idleness.
passages.notes: Sentence begins mid-construction; the opening question ("What?") stands in the preceding context.

passages.original: nisi quia tantae numinum turbae diu frustra fuerat supplicatum, adque ita paulatim loca deserebantur a cultoribus, ut tamquam uacua sine ullius offensione possent humanis saltem usibus uindicari? Namque tunc uelut ad sedandam pestilentiam diligenter repetita adque reparata nisi postea eodem modo neglecta adque usurpata latitarent, non utique magnae peritiae Varronis tribueretur, quod scribens de aedibus sacris tam multa ignorata commemorat. Sed tunc interim elegans non pestilentiae depulsio, sed deorum excusatio procurata est.
passages.english: unless it was because so great a crowd of divinities had long been supplicated in vain, and so the sites were gradually deserted by their worshippers, so that, as if vacant, they could without offending anyone be claimed at least for human uses? For if [the temples], diligently recovered and restored at that time as if to allay the plague, had not afterwards lain hidden, neglected and usurped in the same way, it would certainly not be credited to Varro's great learning that, in writing about sacred buildings, he records so many that were unknown. But meanwhile what was procured at that time was not an elegant removal of the plague but an elegant excuse for the gods.

passages.original: Quam ingrata fuerit Romana ciuitas Scipioni liberatori suo et in quibus moribus egerit, quando eam Sallustius optimam fuisse describit.
passages.english: How ungrateful the Roman state was to Scipio its liberator, and in what morals it lived, at the time when Sallust describes it as having been at its best.
passages.notes: This is a chapter heading.

passages.original: Ultus est huius uictoriae crudelitatem postea Sylla, ne dici quidem opus est quanta deminutione ciuium et quanta calamitate rei publicae). De hac enim uindicta, quae perniciosior fuit, quam si scelera quae puniebantur inpunita relinquerentur, ait et Lucanus: Excessit medicina modum nimiumque secuta est, Qua morbi duxere manum. Periere nocentes; Sed cum iam soli possent superesse nocentes. Illo bello Mariano adque Syllano exceptis his, qui foris in acie ceciderunt, in ipsa quoque Urbe cadaueribus uici plateae fora, theatra templa conpleta sunt, ut difficile iudicaretur, quando uictores plus funerum ediderint, utrum prius ut uincerent, an postea quia uicissent;
passages.english: Sulla afterwards avenged the cruelty of this victory, with what great loss of citizens and what great calamity to the republic there is no need even to say. For of this vengeance, which was more ruinous than if the crimes being punished had been left unpunished, Lucan too says: "The cure exceeded measure and followed too far where the disease led the hand. The guilty perished; but when by then only the guilty could survive." In that war of Marius and Sulla, apart from those who fell in battle outside, in the City itself too the streets, squares, forums, theatres and temples were filled with corpses, so that it was hard to judge when the victors produced more deaths, whether before, in order to win, or afterwards, because they had won;
passages.notes: The opening sentence has a stray closing parenthesis in the text, suggesting a parenthesis whose opening has been lost.

passages.original: An aliud est felicitas, aliud fortuna? Quia fortuna potest esse et mala; felicitas autem si mala fuerit, felicitas non erit. Certe omnes deos utriusque sexus (si et sexum habent) non nisi bonos existimare debemus. Hoc Plato dicit, hoc alii philosophi, hoc excellentes rei publicae populorumque rectores. Quo modo ergo dea Fortuna aliquando bona est, aliquando mala? An forte quando mala est, dea non est, sed in malignum daemonem repente conuertitur?
passages.english: Or is happiness one thing and fortune another? [Yes,] because fortune can also be bad; but happiness, if it were bad, would not be happiness. Certainly we ought to consider all the gods of both sexes (if they also have sex) to be nothing but good. This Plato says, this other philosophers say, this the outstanding rulers of the state and of peoples say. How then is the goddess Fortune sometimes good, sometimes bad? Or perhaps, when she is bad, is she not a goddess, but suddenly turned into a malignant demon?

passages.original: Sed (fingebat haec Homerus, ait Tullius, et humana ad deos transferebat: diuina mallem ad nos.\' Merito displicuit uiro graui diuinorum criminum poeta confictor. Quur ergo ludi scaenici, ubi haec dictitantur cantitantur actitantur, deorum honoribus exhibentur, inter res diuinas a doctissimis conscribuntur?
passages.english: But "Homer," says Tullius, "invented these things and transferred human things to the gods: I would rather [he had transferred] divine things to us." Rightly did the poet who fabricated crimes of the gods displease a serious man. Why then are stage plays, where these things are constantly said, sung and acted, presented in honour of the gods, and listed by the most learned among divine matters?
passages.notes: The opening parenthesis before 'fingebat' in the edition is unmatched; treated as the start of the quotation from Cicero.

passages.original: Cicero augur inridet auguria et inridet homines corui et corniculae uocibus uitae consilia moderantes. Sed iste Academicus, qui omnia esse contendit incerta, indignus est qui habeat ullam in his rebus auctoritatem. Disputat aput eum Quintus Lucilius Balbus in secundo de deorum natura libro, et cum ipse superstitiones ex natura rerum uelut physicas et philosophicas inserat, indignatur tamen institutioni simulacrorum et opinionibus fabulosis ita loquens: \'Videtisne igitur, ut a physicis rebus bene adque utiliter inuentis ratio sit tracta ad commenticios et fictos deos?
passages.english: Cicero, an augur, mocks augury and mocks people who regulate the decisions of their lives by the cries of a raven and a crow. But this Academic, who maintains that all things are uncertain, does not deserve to have any authority in these matters. In his work, Quintus Lucilius Balbus argues in the second book On the Nature of the Gods, and although he himself introduces superstitions drawn from the nature of things as if they were physical and philosophical, he is nevertheless indignant at the setting up of images and at mythical opinions, speaking thus: 'Do you see, then, how from physical things well and usefully discovered reasoning was drawn off to invented and fictitious gods?

passages.original: Et formae enim nobis deorum et aetates et uestitus ornatusque noti sunt, genera praeterea, coniugia, cognationes, omniaque traducta ad similitudinem inbecillitatis humanae. Nam et perturbatis animis inducuntur; accepimus enim deorum cupiditates aegritudines iracundias. Nec uero, ut fabulae ferunt, di bellis proeliisque caruerunt; nec solum, ut aput Homerum, \'cum duos exercitus contrarios alii di ex alia parte defenderent, sed etiam (ut cum Titanis aut cum Gigantibus) sua propria bella gesserunt. Haec et dicuntur et creduntur stultissime et plena sunt uanitatis summaeque leuitatis.\' Ecce interim quae confitentur qui defendunt deos gentium.
passages.english: "For the shapes of the gods are known to us, and their ages, clothing and adornment, and moreover their lineages, marriages, kinships, and everything carried over into the likeness of human weakness. For they are also represented with disturbed minds; for we have heard of the lusts, griefs and rages of the gods. Nor indeed, as the stories relate, were the gods free of wars and battles; and not only, as in Homer, when different gods defended two opposing armies from opposite sides, but they even waged their own wars (as with the Titans or with the Giants). These things are both said and believed most foolishly, and are full of emptiness and the utmost frivolity." See meanwhile what those who defend the gods of the nations admit.

passages.original: Cicero dicit Hippocratem, nobilissimum medicum, scriptum reliquisse, quosdam fratres, cum simul aegrotare coepissent et eorum morbus eodem tempore ingrauesceret, eodem leuaretur, geminos suspicatum; quos Posidonius Stoicus, multum astrologiae deditus, eadem constitutione astrorum natos eademque conceptos solebat adserere. Ita quod medicus pertinere credebat ad simillimam temperiem ualetudinis, hoc philosophus astrologus ad uim constitutionemque siderum, quae fuerat quo tempore concepti natique sunt.
passages.english: Cicero says that Hippocrates, a most famous physician, left it in writing that he suspected certain brothers were twins, since they had begun to fall ill together and their illness grew worse at the same time and was relieved at the same time; these Posidonius the Stoic, much given to astrology, used to assert had been born under the same arrangement of the stars and conceived under the same. So what the physician believed related to a very similar balance of health, the philosopher-astrologer [attributed] to the power and arrangement of the stars as it had been at the time when they were conceived and born.

passages.original: Illi quoque uersus Homerici huic sententiae suffragantur, quos Cicero in Latinum uertit: Tales sunt hominum mentes, quali pater ipse Iuppiter Iuppiter lustrauit lumine terras. Nec in hac quaestione auctoritatem haberet poetica sententia: sed quoniam Stoicos dicit uim fati adserentes istos ex Homero uersus solere usurpare, non de illius poetae, sed de istorum philosophorum opinione tractatur, cum per istos uersus, quos disputationi adhibent quam de fato habent, quid sentiant esse fatum apertissime declaratur, quoniam Iouem appellant, quem summum deum putant, a quo conexionem dicunt pendere fatorum.
passages.english: Those lines of Homer also support this view, which Cicero translated into Latin: "Such are the minds of men as the light with which father Jupiter himself has illumined the earth." Nor would a poetic saying carry authority in this question; but since he says that the Stoics, asserting the power of fate, are accustomed to use these lines from Homer, the discussion is not about that poet's opinion but about those philosophers', since through these lines, which they bring into the disputation they hold about fate, it is most plainly declared what they think fate is, since they name Jupiter, whom they consider the highest god, on whom they say the chain of fates depends.
passages.notes: 'Iuppiter Iuppiter' is a dittography in the text; translated once.

passages.original: Laudat idem Sallustius temporibus suis magnos et praeclaros uiros, Marcum Catonem et Gaium Caesarem, dicens quod diu illa res publica non habuit quemquam uirtute magnum, sed sua memoria fuisse illos duos ingenti uirtute, diuersis moribus. In laudibus autem Caesaris posuit, quod sibi magnum imperium, exercitum, bellum nouum exoptabat, ubi uirtus enitescere posset.
passages.english: The same Sallust praises great and illustrious men of his own times, Marcus Cato and Gaius Caesar, saying that for a long time that commonwealth had not had anyone great in virtue, but that within his memory there had been those two of immense virtue, of differing characters. And among the praises of Caesar he set down that he longed for a great command, an army, a new war for himself, where his virtue could shine forth.

passages.original: Sed cum illa memoria duo Romani essent uirtute magni, Caesar et Cato, longe uirtus Catonis ueritati uidetur propinquior fuisse quam Caesaris. Proinde qualis esset illo tempore ciuitas et antea qualis fuisset, uideamus in ipsa sententia Catonis: \'Nolite, inquit, existimare maiores nostros armis rem publicam ex parua magnam fecisse. Si ita esset, multo pulcherrimam eam nos haberemus. Quippe sociorum adque ciuium, praeterea armorum et equorum maior copia nobis quam illis est.
passages.english: But though within that memory there were two Romans great in virtue, Caesar and Cato, the virtue of Cato seems to have been far nearer to the truth than Caesar's. Accordingly, let us see what the city was like at that time and what it had been before, in Cato's own speech: "Do not think," he says, "that our ancestors made the commonwealth great from small by arms. If that were so, we would have it most beautiful by far. For we have a greater supply of allies and citizens, and moreover of arms and horses, than they did.

passages.original: Qui audit haec Catonis uerba siue Sallustii, putat, quales laudantur Romani ueteres, omnes eos tales tunc fuisse uel plures. Non ita est; alioquin uera non essent, quae ipse item scribit, ea quae commemoraui in secundo libro huius operis, ubi dicit, iniurias ualidiorum et ob eas discessionem plebis a patribus aliasque dissensiones domi fuisse iam inde a principio, neque amplius aequo et modesto iure actum quam expulsis regibus quamdiu metus a Tarquinio fuit, donec bellum graue, quod propter ipsum cum Etruria susceptum fuerat, finiretur;
passages.english: Whoever hears these words of Cato, or of Sallust, thinks that the ancient Romans who are praised were all such at that time, or most of them. It is not so; otherwise the things he himself likewise writes would not be true, those which I recalled in the second book of this work, where he says that the injuries done by the stronger, and because of them the secession of the plebs from the patricians and other dissensions at home, existed right from the beginning, and that matters were conducted with fair and moderate justice no longer after the expulsion of the kings than as long as there was fear of Tarquin, until the heavy war which had been undertaken with Etruria on his account was ended;

passages.original: Quam ob rem quam diu fuissent regna Orientis inlustria, uoluit Deus et Occidentale fieri, quod tempore esset posterius, sed imperii latitudine et magnitudine inlustrius, idque talibus potissimum concessit hominibus ad domanda grauia mala multarum gentium, qui causa honoris laudis et gloriae consuluerunt patriae, in qua ipsam gloriam requirebant, salutemque eius saluti suae praeponere non dubitauerunt, pro isto uno uitio, id est amore laudis, pecuniae cupiditatem et multa alia uitia conprimentes. Nam sanius uidet, qui et amorem laudis uitium esse cognoscit, quod nec poetam fugit Horatium, qui ait: Laudis amore tumes: sunt certa piacula, quae te Ter pure lecto poterunt recreare libello. Idemque in carmine lyrico ad reprimendam dominandi libidinem ita cecinit: Latius regnes auidum domando Spiritum, quam si Libyam remotis Gadibus iungas et uterque Poenus Seruiat uni.
passages.english: Therefore, when the kingdoms of the East had been illustrious for a long time, God willed that a Western one should also arise, which was later in time but more illustrious in the breadth and greatness of its empire; and he granted it especially to such men, for subduing the grievous evils of many nations, as for the sake of honour, praise and glory took counsel for their fatherland, in which they sought that very glory, and did not hesitate to put its safety before their own, suppressing for the sake of this one vice, that is the love of praise, the desire for money and many other vices. For he sees more soundly who recognises that the love of praise too is a vice, which did not escape the poet Horace either, who says: "You swell with love of praise: there are sure expiations which can restore you, a little book read three times with purity." And the same man in a lyric poem sang thus to restrain the lust for domination: "You would rule more widely by taming a greedy spirit than if you joined Libya to distant Gades, and each Carthaginian served one [master]."

passages.original: Nam licet procliue sit, ut, qui humana gloria nimium delectatur, etiam dominari ardenter adfectet, tamen qui ueram licet humanarum laudum gloriam concupiscunt, dant operam bene iudicantibus non displicere. Sunt enim multa in moribus bona, de quibus multi bene iudicant, quamuis ea multi non habeant; per ea bona morum nituntur ad gloriam et imperium uel dominationem, de quibus ait Sallustius: \'Sed ille uera uia nititur.) Quisquis autem sine cupiditate gloriae, qua ueretur homo bene iudicantibus displicere, dominari adque imperare desiderat, etiam per apertissima scelera quaerit plerumque obtinere quod diligit.
passages.english: For although it is an easy slope for one who delights too much in human glory to aspire ardently also to domination, yet those who desire true glory, albeit of human praise, take care not to displease those who judge well. For there are many good things in character, about which many judge well, although many do not possess them; by these good qualities of character they strive for glory and command or domination, of whom Sallust says: "But that one strives by the true way." But whoever desires to dominate and command without the desire for glory, by which a man fears to displease those who judge well, mostly seeks to obtain what he loves even by the most open crimes.

passages.original: Aperta de hac re uox diuina est loquente Dei sapientia: Per me reges regnant et tyranni per me tenent terram. Sed ne tyranni non pessimi adque inprobi reges, sed uetere nomine fortes dicti existimentur (unde ait Vergilius: Pars mihi pacis erit dextram tetigisse tyranni): apertissime alio loco de Deo dictum est: Quia regnare facit hominem hypocritam propter peruersitatem populi. Quam ob rem, quamuis ut potui satis exposuerim qua causa Deus unus uerus et iustus Romanos secundum quandam formam terrenae ciuitatis bonos adiuuerit ad tanti imperii gloriam consequendam: potest tamen et alia causa esse latentior propter diuersa merita generis humani, Deo magis nota quam nobis, dum illud constet inter omnes ueraciter pios, neminem sine uera pietate, id est ueri Dei uero cultu, ueram posse habere uirtutem, nec eam ueram esse, quando gloriae seruit humanae;
passages.english: On this matter the divine voice is plain, when the Wisdom of God says: "By me kings reign, and by me tyrants hold the land." But so that "tyrants" should not be thought to mean here, not the worst and wicked kings, but, in the old sense of the word, strong men (hence Virgil says: "It will be a part of peace for me to have touched the right hand of the tyrant"), it is said most plainly of God in another place: "Who makes a hypocrite reign because of the perversity of the people." Therefore, although I have explained as well as I could why the one true and just God helped the Romans, who were good according to a certain pattern of the earthly city, to attain the glory of so great an empire, there can nevertheless be another, more hidden cause, on account of the differing merits of the human race, better known to God than to us; provided that this is agreed among all who are truly pious: that no one can have true virtue without true piety, that is, without the true worship of the true God, and that virtue is not true when it serves human glory;
passages.notes: Scriptural quotations are Prov. 8:15–16 and Job 34:30; Virgil, Aeneid 7.266.

passages.original: Qui tametsi minus est suauis eloquio, doctrina tamen adque sententiis ita refertus est, ut in omni eruditione, quam nos saecularem, illi autem liberalem uocant, studiosum rerum tantum iste doceat, quantum studiosum -uerborum Cicero delectat. Denique et ipse [Tullius] huic tale testimonium perhibet, ut in libris Academicis dicat eam, quae ibi uersatur, disputationem se habuisse cum Marco Varrone, (homine, inquit, omnium facile acutissimo et sine ulla dubitatione doctissimo). Non ait \'eloquentissimo\' uel (facundissimo), quoniam re uera in hac facultate multum inpar est; sed \'omnium, inquit, facile acutissimo), et in eis libris. id est Academicis, ubi cuncta dubitanda esse contendit, addidit \'sine ulla dubitatione doctissimo\'.
passages.english: Though he is less pleasing in style, he is so packed with learning and ideas that in all the scholarship which we call secular, but they call liberal, he teaches the student of things as much as Cicero delights the student of words. Indeed Tullius himself gives him such testimony that he says in his Academic books that the discussion carried on there he had held with Marcus Varro, "a man," he says, "easily the sharpest of all and without any doubt the most learned." He does not say "most eloquent" or "most fluent," since in truth he is very unequal in this faculty; but he says "easily the sharpest of all," and in those books, that is the Academics, where he argues that everything is to be doubted, he added "without any doubt the most learned."
passages.notes: "[Tullius]" is bracketed in the edition, presumably as a suspected addition.

passages.original: tu sacerdotum, tu domesticam, tu publicam disciplinam, tu sedem regionum locorum, tu omnium diuinarum humanarumque rerum nomina genera, officia causas aperuisti.\' Iste igitur uir tam insignis excellentisque peritiae et, quod de illo etiam Terentianus elegantissimo uel\'siculo breuiter ait: Vir doctissimus undecumque Varro, qui tam multa legit, ut aliquid ei scribere uacuisse miremur; tam multa scripsit, quam multa uix quemquam legere potuisse credamus: iste, inquam, uir tantus ingenio tantusque doctrina, si rerum uelut diuinarum, de quibus scribit, obpugnator esset adque destructor easque non ad religionem, sed ad superstitionem diceret pertinere, nescio utrum tam multa in eis ridenda contemnenda detestanda conscriberet.
passages.english: you have disclosed the [law] of priests, domestic and public discipline, the location of regions and places, the names, kinds, functions and causes of all things divine and human.' This man, then, of such distinguished and excellent learning, of whom Terentianus also says briefly in a most elegant little verse, 'Varro, a man most learned in every respect', who read so much that we marvel he had any time to write, and wrote so much that we can scarcely believe anyone could have read it: this man, I say, so great in intellect and so great in learning, if he were an opponent and destroyer of the so-called divine things about which he writes, and said that they belonged not to religion but to superstition, I do not know whether he would have written down so many things in them that are laughable, contemptible and detestable.
passages.notes: 'uel\'siculo' is a scanning error for 'versiculo' (little verse). The opening continues Cicero's list of Varro's achievements from the preceding context.

passages.original: De tribus generibus theologiae secundum Varronem, id est uno fabuloso, altero naturali tertioque ciuili.
passages.english: On the three kinds of theology according to Varro, that is, one mythical, the second natural, and the third civil.
passages.notes: Chapter heading.

passages.original: \'Secundum genus est, inquit, quod demonstraui, de quo multos libros philosophi reliquerunt; in quibus est, di qui sint, ubi, quod genus, quale; a quodam tempore an a sempiterno fuerint di; ex igni sint, ut credit Heraclitus, an ex numeris, ut Pythagoras, an ex atomis, ut ait Epicurus. Sic alia, quae facilius intra parietes in schola quam extra in foro ferre possunt aures). Nihil in hoc genere culpauit, quod physicon uocant et ad philosophos pertinet, tantum quod eorum inter se controuersias commemorauit, per quos facta est dissidentium multitudo sectarum.
passages.english: "The second kind," he says, "which I have pointed out, is the one about which philosophers have left many books; in them is discussed who the gods are, where, of what kind, of what quality; whether the gods have existed from a certain time or from eternity; whether they are made of fire, as Heraclitus believes, or of numbers, as Pythagoras, or of atoms, as Epicurus says. And other such things, which ears can bear more easily within walls in a school than outside in the forum." He found nothing to blame in this kind, which they call physical and which belongs to the philosophers, except that he mentioned their controversies among themselves, through which a multitude of dissenting sects has arisen.

passages.original: Multi enim et ipsa ad eundem modum interpretati sunt, usque adeo ut, quod ab eis inmanissimum et infandissimum dicitur, Saturnum suos filios deuorasse, ita nonnulli interpretentur, quod longinquitas temporis, quae Saturni nomine significatur, quidquid gignit ipsa consumat, uel, sicut idem opinatur Varro, quod pertineat Saturnus ad semina, quae in terram, de qua oriuntur, iterum recidunt. Itemque alii alio modo et similiter cetera.
passages.english: For many have interpreted these [rites] too in the same way, to such an extent that what they call the most monstrous and unspeakable thing, that Saturn devoured his own sons, some interpret thus: that the length of time, which is signified by the name of Saturn, consumes whatever it begets; or, as the same Varro thinks, that Saturn pertains to seeds, which fall back again into the earth from which they spring. And others [interpret it] in another way, and likewise with the rest.

passages.original: Fieri enim potest, ut saltem deos selectos adque praecipuos, quos Varro uolumine conplexus est ultimo, de quibus parum diximus, quisquam colendos propter uitam beatam, quae non nisi aeterna est, opinetur. Qua in re non dico quod facetius ait Tertullianus fortasse quam uerius: Si di eliguntur ut bulbi, utique ceteri reprobi iudicantur. Non hoc dico: uideo enim etiam ex selectis selegi aliquos ad aliquid maius adque praestantius, sicut in militia, cum tirones electi fuerint, ex his quoque eliguntur ad opus aliquod maius armorum;
passages.english: For it may be that someone thinks at least the select and principal gods, whom Varro covered in his last volume and about whom we have said little, ought to be worshipped for the sake of the blessed life, which is none other than eternal. On this point I do not say what Tertullian said, perhaps more wittily than truly: "If gods are selected like onions, then the rest are surely judged rejects." I do not say this, for I see that even from the select some are selected for something greater and more excellent, as in the army, when recruits have been selected, from these too some are selected for some greater work of arms;
passages.notes: bulbi: bulbs, i.e. onions or similar.

passages.original: Cum igitur in his minutis operibus, quae minutatim dis pluribus distributa sunt, etiam ipsos selectos uideamus tamquam senatum cum plebe pariter operari, et inueniamus a quibusdam dis, qui nequaquam seligendi putati sunt, multa maiora adque meliora administrari quam ab illis, qui selecti uocantur: restat arbitrari non propter praestantiores in mundo administrationes, sed quia prouenit eis, ut magis populis innotescerent, selectos eos et praecipuos nuncupatos. Unde dicit etiam ipse Varro, quod dis quibusdam patribus et deabus matribus, sicut hominibus, ignobilitas accidisset. Si ergo Felicitas ideo fortasse inter selectos deos esse non debuit, quod ad istam nobilitatem non merito, sed fortuito peruenerunt: saltem inter illos uel potius prae illis Fortuna poneretur, quam dicunt deam non rationabili dispositione, sed ut temere acciderit, sua cuique dona conferre.
passages.english: Since, then, in these petty tasks that have been distributed piecemeal among many gods, we see even the select gods themselves working alongside, like a senate with the common people, and we find that many greater and better things are administered by certain gods who were by no means thought worth selecting than by those who are called select, it remains to conclude that they were named select and chief not because of more eminent administrations in the world, but because it happened to them to become better known to the peoples. Hence Varro himself also says that obscurity had befallen certain father gods and mother goddesses, just as it does men. If, then, Felicity perhaps ought not to have been among the select gods because they reached that distinction not by merit but by chance, at least Fortune should have been placed among them, or rather ahead of them, the goddess who, they say, confers her gifts on each not by rational arrangement but as it happens at random.

passages.original: Sed ipsorum potius interpretationes physicas audiamus, quibus turpitudinem miserrimi erroris uelut altioris doctrinae specie colorare conantur. Primum eas interpretationes sic Varro commendat, ut dicat antiquos simulacra deorum et insignia ornatusque finxisse, quae cum oculis animaduertissent hi, qui adissent doctrinae mysteria, possent animam mundi ac partes eius, id est deos ueros, animo uidere;
passages.english: But let us rather hear their physical interpretations, by which they try to colour the shamefulness of a most wretched error with the appearance, as it were, of a deeper doctrine. First, Varro commends these interpretations by saying that the ancients fashioned images of the gods, and their insignia and adornments, so that those who had approached the mysteries of the doctrine, when they had observed them with their eyes, might see with the mind the soul of the world and its parts, that is, the true gods;

passages.original: Dicit ergo idem Varro adhuc de naturali theologia praeloquens deum se arbitrari esse animam mundi, quem Graeci uocant xo[i.ov, et hunc ipsum mundum esse deum; sed sicut hominem sapientem, cum sit ex corpore et animo, tamen ab animo dici sapientem, ita mundum deum dici ab animo, cum sit ex animo et corpore.
passages.english: So the same Varro, still speaking by way of preface about natural theology, says that he thinks God is the soul of the world, which the Greeks call *kosmos*, and that this world itself is God; but that just as a wise man, though he consists of body and mind, is nevertheless called wise from his mind, so the world is called God from its mind, though it consists of mind and body.
passages.notes: "xo[i.ov" is a scanning garble of the Greek κόσμον (kosmon), 'world'.

passages.original: Iouem autem, qui etiam Iuppiter dicitur, quem uelint in-; tellegi, exponant. \'Deus est, inquiunt, habens potestatem can-\', sarum, quibus aliquid fit in mundo.\' Hoc quam magnum sit,I nobilissimus Vergilii uersus ille testatur: Felix qui potuit rerum cognoscere causas. Sed quur ei praeponitur Ianus? hoc nobis uir ille acutissimus doctissimusque respondeat. \'Quoniam penes lacum, inquit, sunt prima, penes louem summa. Merito ergo rex omnium Iuppiter habetur. Prima enim uincuntur a summis, quia, licet prima praecedant tempore, summa superant dignitate.\' Sed recte hoc diceretur, si factorum prima discernerentur et summa;
passages.english: Let them explain whom they mean to be understood by Jove, who is also called Jupiter. "He is the god," they say, "who has power over the causes by which anything comes about in the world." How great this is that most famous line of Virgil attests: "Happy he who has been able to know the causes of things." But why is Janus placed before him? Let that most acute and learned man answer us. "Because," he says, "first things are in the power of Janus, highest things in the power of Jupiter. Rightly therefore Jupiter is held king of all. For first things are surpassed by highest things, since, although first things precede in time, highest things excel in dignity." But this would be rightly said if first and highest were distinguished among things done;
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: can-sarum = causarum, lacum/louem = Ianum/Iouem.

passages.original: Ergo et Iouem, ut deus sit et maxime rex deorum, non alium possunt existimare quam mundum, ut dis ceteris secundum istos suis partibus regnet. In hanc sententiam etiam quosdam uersus Valerii Sorani exponit idem Varro in eo libro, quem seorsum ab istis de cultu deorum scripsit; qui uersus hi sunt: Iuppiter omnipotens regum rerumque deumque Progenitor genetrixquo deum, deus unus et omnes. Exponuntur autem in eodem libro ita: cum marem existimarent qui semen emitteret, feminam quae acciperet, Iouemque esse mundum et eum omnia semina ex se emittere et in se recipere, \'cum causa, inquit, scripsit Soranus: Iuppiter progenitor genetrixque;
passages.english: Therefore they cannot suppose Jupiter too, in order that he may be a god and above all the king of the gods, to be anything other than the world, so that, according to these people, he may reign over the other gods, who are his parts. In support of this view the same Varro also expounds certain verses of Valerius Soranus in the book which he wrote separately from these on the worship of the gods; the verses are these: "Almighty Jupiter, progenitor of kings and things and gods, and mother of the gods, god one and all." They are expounded in the same book as follows: since they considered the male to be the one who emits seed and the female the one who receives it, and that Jupiter is the world and that he emits all seeds from himself and receives them into himself, "not without reason," he says, "did Soranus write: 'Jupiter progenitor and mother';
passages.notes: "genetrixquo" read as "genetrixque". "cum causa" taken as 'with reason'.

passages.original: Et sicut haec, quae exempli gratia commemoraui, ita cetera non explicant, sed potius inplicant; sicut impetus errabundae opinionis inpulerit, ita huc adque illuc, hinc adque illinc insiliunt et resiliunt, ut ipse Varro de omnibus dubitare quam aliquid adfirmare maluerit. Nam trium extremorum primum de dis certis cum absoluisset librum, in altero de dis incertis dicere ingressus ait: \'Cum in hoc libello dubias de dis opiniones posuero, reprehendi non debeo.
passages.english: And just as with these things, which I have mentioned by way of example, so with the rest they do not explain but rather entangle; as the impulse of wandering opinion has driven them, so they leap this way and that, hither and thither, forward and back, so that Varro himself preferred to doubt about everything rather than affirm anything. For when he had finished the first of the last three books, on the certain gods, in the second, beginning to speak about the uncertain gods, he says: "When in this little book I set down doubtful opinions about the gods, I ought not to be blamed.

passages.original: In tertio porro isto de dis selectis, postea quam praelocutus est quod ex naturali theologia praeloquendum putauit, ingressurus huius ciuilis theologiae uanitates et insanias mendaces, ubi eum non solum non ducebat rerum ueritas, sed etiam maiorum premebat auctoritas: \'De dis, inquit, populi Romani publicis, quibus aedes dedicauerunt eosque pluribus signis ornatos notauerunt, in hoc libro scribam, sed ut Xenophanes Colophonius scribit, quid putem, non quid contendam, ponam. Hominis est enim haec opinari, dei scire\'. Rerum igitur non conprehensarum nec firmissime creditarum, sed opinatarum et dubitandarum sermonem trepidus pollicetur dicturus ea, quae ab hominibus instituta sunt.
passages.english: Further, in this third book, on the select gods, after he had said by way of preface what he thought needed to be said beforehand from natural theology, being about to enter upon the vanities and lying insanities of this civil theology, where not only did the truth of things not lead him, but the authority of the ancestors also pressed upon him, he says: "In this book I shall write about the public gods of the Roman people, to whom they have dedicated temples and whom they have marked out, adorned with many images; but, as Xenophanes of Colophon writes, I shall set down what I think, not what I maintain. For it belongs to man to have opinions about these things, to God to know." So he fearfully promises a discourse about things not grasped nor most firmly believed, but held as opinions and open to doubt, as he is about to speak of things that were instituted by men.

passages.original: De Terra, quam Varro deam esse confirmat, eo quod ille animus mundi, quem opinatur deum, etiam hanc corporis sui infimam partem permeet eique uim diuinam inpertiat.
passages.english: On Earth, whom Varro affirms to be a goddess, on the ground that that soul of the world, which he supposes to be God, also pervades this lowest part of its body and imparts divine power to it.
passages.notes: A chapter heading.

passages.original: Hinc etiam Samothracum nobilia mysteria in superiore libro sic interpretatur eaque se, quae nec suis nota sunt, scribendo expositurum eisque missurum quasi religiosissime pollicetur. Dicit enim se ibi multis indiciis collegisse in simulacris aliud significare caelum, aliud terram, aliud exempla rerum, quas Plato appellat ideas; caelum Iouem, terram Iunonem, ideas Mineruam uult intellegi; caelum a quo fiat aliquid, terram de qua fiat, exemplum secundum quod fiat. Qua in re omitto dicere, quod Plato illas ideas tantam uim habere dicit, ut secundum eas non caelum aliquid fecerit, sed etiam caelum factum sit.
passages.english: On this basis he also interprets the famous mysteries of the Samothracians in an earlier book, and promises, as if most religiously, that he will explain them in writing and send them to [people] to whom they are not known even among their own. For he says that he has gathered there from many indications that among the images one signifies the sky, another the earth, another the patterns of things, which Plato calls ideas; by the sky he wants Jupiter understood, by the earth Juno, by the ideas Minerva; the sky by which something is made, the earth from which it is made, the pattern according to which it is made. In this matter I pass over saying that Plato says those ideas have such power that according to them not the sky made anything, but even the sky itself was made.
passages.notes: "eisque missurum… quae nec suis nota sunt" is compressed; sense is that he would send the explanation to those (initiates) to whom these things are not known.

passages.original: Nihil autem huic operi, quod mundo considerato tam mirabile aspicimus, ex diuina mente praeposuit. Huic successit Anaximander, eius auditor, mutauitque de rerum natura opinionem. Non enim ex una re, sicut Thales ex umore, sed ex suis propriis principiis quasque res nasci putauit. Quae rerum principia singularum esse credidit infinita, et innumerabiles mundos gignere et quaecumque in eis oriuntur; eosque mundos modo dissolui, modo iterum gigni existimauit, quanta quisque aetate sua manere potuerit;
passages.english: But he set nothing from a divine mind over this work which, considering the world, we behold as so wonderful. Anaximander, his pupil, succeeded him and changed the opinion about the nature of things. For he thought that each thing is born not from one thing, as Thales [thought] from moisture, but from its own proper principles. These principles of individual things he believed to be infinite, and to generate innumerable worlds and whatever arises in them; and he thought those worlds are now dissolved, now born again, according to how long each could last in its own age;

passages.original: Tam praeclara igitur uitae mortisque fama Socrates reliquit plurimos suae philosophiae sectatores, quorum certatim studium fuit in quaestionum moralium disceptatione uersari, ubi agitur de summo bono, quo fieri homo beatus potest. Quod in Socratis disputationibus, dum omnia mouet adserit destruit, quoniam non euidenter apparuit, quod cuique placuit inde sumserunt et ubi cuique uisum est constituerunt finem boni. Finis autem boni appellatur, quo quisque cum peruenerit beatus est. Sic autem diuersas inter se Socratici de isto fine sententias habuerunt, ut (quod uix credibile est unius magistri potuisse facere sectatores) quidam summum bonum esse dicerent uoluptatem, sicut Aristippus;
passages.english: So Socrates, having left behind so illustrious a reputation in life and death, left very many followers of his philosophy, whose zeal was to vie with one another in occupying themselves with the discussion of moral questions, where the subject is the highest good, by which a man can become happy. Since this did not appear clearly in Socrates' discussions, as he raised, asserted and demolished everything, each took from them what pleased him and each set the end of the good where it seemed best to him. Now the end of the good is the name for that which, when anyone has attained it, he is happy. And the Socratics held opinions on this end so different from one another that (which is scarcely credible that followers of a single master could have done) some said that the highest good was pleasure, as Aristippus did;

passages.original: Cum enim magistri sui Socratis, quem facit in suis uoluminibus disputantem, notissimum morem dissimulandae scientiae uel opinionis suae seruare adfectat, quia et illi iste mos placuit, factum est ut etiam ipsius Platonis de rebus magnis sententiae non facile perspici possint. Ex his tamen, quae aput eum leguntur, siue quae dixit, siue quae ab aliis dicta esse narrauit adque conscripsit, quae sibi placita uiderentur, quaedam commemorari et operi huic inseri oportet a nobis, uel ubi suffragatur religioni uerae, quam fides nostra suscipit ac defendit, uel ubi ei uidetur esse contrarius, quantum ad istam de uno Deo et pluribus pertinet quaestionem, propter uitam, quae post mortem futura est, ueraciter beatam.
passages.english: For since he aims to keep the well-known habit of his master Socrates, whom he presents in his volumes as the speaker, of concealing his knowledge or opinion, because that habit pleased him too, it has come about that even Plato's own views on great matters cannot easily be discerned. Yet from what is read in him, whether what he said, or what he related and wrote down as said by others that seemed acceptable to him, some things ought to be mentioned and inserted into this work by us, either where he supports the true religion which our faith takes up and defends, or where he seems contrary to it, so far as concerns this question of the one God and many, for the sake of the truly blessed life that is to come after death.

passages.original: Timens enim et ille quasi reuelata mysteria petens admonet Alexandrum, ut, cum ea matri conscripta insinuauerit, flammis iubeat concremari.) Non solum ergo ista, quae duae theologiae, fabulosa continet et ciuilis, Platonicis philosophis cedant, qui uerum Deum et rerum auctorem et ueritatis inlustratorem et beatitudinis largitorem esse dixerunt; sed alii quoque philosophi, qui corporalia naturae principia corpori deditis mentibus opinati sunt, cedant his tantis et tanti Dei cognitoribus uiris, ut Thales in umore, Anaximenes in aere, Stoici in igne, Epicurus in atomis, hoc est minutissimis corpusculis, quae nec diuidi nec sentiri queunt, et quicumque alii, quorum enumeratione inmorari non est necesse, siue simplicia siue coniuncta corpora, siue uita carentia siue uiuentia, sed tamen corpora, causam principiumque rerum esse dixerunt.
passages.english: For he too, fearing, as if begging [him] about mysteries revealed, warns Alexander that, when he has made them known to his mother in writing, he should order [the letter] burnt in the flames.) So not only should these things contained in the two theologies, the mythical and the civil, yield to the Platonic philosophers, who said that the true God is the author of things, the illuminator of truth and the bestower of blessedness; but the other philosophers too, who with minds given over to the body held bodily principles of nature, should yield to these men so great and knowers of so great a God: such as Thales in moisture, Anaximenes in air, the Stoics in fire, Epicurus in atoms, that is the tiniest little bodies, which can be neither divided nor perceived, and whoever else, whom there is no need to linger in listing, said that bodies, whether simple or compound, whether lifeless or living, but still bodies, are the cause and principle of things.
passages.notes: The opening refers to the letter of Alexander the Great to his mother; "he" is presumably the Egyptian priest Leo. The closing parenthesis closes an aside begun before the passage.

passages.original: Nam et ipsi, qui res non amandas amant, non se beatos putant amando, sed fruendo. Quisquis ergo fruitur eo, quod amat, uerumque et summum bonum amat, quis eum beatum nisi miserrimus negat? Ipsum autem uerum ac summum bonum Plato dicit Deum, unde uult esse philosophum amatorem Dei, ut, quoniam philosophia ad beatam uitam tendit, fruens Deo sit beatus qui Deum amauerit.
passages.english: For even those who love things not to be loved think themselves blessed not by loving but by enjoying. Whoever, then, enjoys what he loves, and loves the true and highest good, who but the most wretched would deny that he is blessed? Now this true and highest good Plato says is God, which is why he wants the philosopher to be a lover of God, so that, since philosophy aims at the blessed life, whoever has loved God may be blessed by enjoying God.

passages.original: Quicumque igitur philosophi de Deo summo et uero ista senserunt, quod et rerum creatarum sit effector et lumen cognoscendarum et bonum agendarum, quod ab illo nobis sit et principium naturae et ueritas doctrinae et felicitas uitae, siue Platonici adcommodatius nuncupentur, siue quodlibet aliud sectae suae nomen inponant; siue tantummodo Ionici generis, qui in eis praecipui fuerunt, ista senserint, sicut idem Plato et qui eum bene intellexerunt; siue etiam Italici, propter Pythagoram et Pythagoreos et si qui forte alii eiusdem sententiae indidem fuerunt; siue aliarum quoque gentium qui sapientes uel philosophi habiti sunt, Atlantici Libyes, Aegyptii, Indi, Persae, Chaldaei, Scythae, Galli, Hispani aliqui reperiuntur, qui hoc uiderint ac docuerint: eos omnes ceteris anteponimus eosque nobis propinquiores fatemur.
passages.english: Whatever philosophers, then, have held these views about the supreme and true God, that he is the maker of created things, the light by which things are known, and the good for which things are done, that from him we have the origin of our nature, the truth of our learning, and the happiness of our life, whether they are more fittingly called Platonists, or give their school some other name; whether only those of the Ionian kind who were preeminent among them held these views, as Plato himself and those who understood him well did; or also those of the Italian kind, on account of Pythagoras and the Pythagoreans and any others perhaps of the same opinion from the same place; or whether among other nations too some are found who were reckoned wise men or philosophers, Atlantic Libyans, Egyptians, Indians, Persians, Chaldaeans, Scythians, Gauls, Spaniards, who saw and taught this: all these we place above the rest, and we acknowledge them to be nearer to us.

passages.original: unde putatur sic intellexisse quod scriptum est: spiritus Dei superferebatur super aquam. Parum quippe adtendens quo more soleat illa scriptura appellare spiritum Dei, quoniam et aer spiritus dicitur, quattuor opinatus elementa loco illo commemorata uideri potest Deinde quod Plato dicit amatorem Dei esse philosophum, nihil sic illis sacris litteris flagrat; et maxime illud (quod et me plurimum adducit, ut paene adsentiar Platonem illorum librorum expertem non fuisse), quod, cum ad sanctum Moysen ita uerba Dei per angelum perferantur, ut quaerenti quod sit nomen eius, qui eum pergere praecipiebat ad populum Hebraeum ex Aegypto liberandum, respondeatur: Ego sum qui sum, et dices filiis Israel: Qui est, misit me ad uos, tamquam in eius conparatione, qui uere est quia incommutabilis est, ea quae mutabilia facta sunt non sint, uehementer hoc Plato tenuit et diligentissime commendauit.
passages.english: From this he is thought to have understood in this way what is written: "The Spirit of God was borne over the water." For, paying too little attention to the way that scripture usually names the Spirit of God, since air too is called spirit, he may seem to have thought that the four elements were mentioned in that place. Then, as to Plato's saying that the philosopher is a lover of God, nothing burns so brightly in those sacred writings; and above all this (which also most strongly inclines me almost to agree that Plato was not unacquainted with those books): when the words of God were conveyed through an angel to holy Moses, so that when he asked what was the name of him who was commanding him to go and free the Hebrew people from Egypt, the answer was given: "I am who am, and you shall say to the children of Israel: He who is has sent me to you," as if, in comparison with him who truly is because he is unchangeable, the things that have been made changeable are not, this Plato held vehemently and commended most diligently.
