passages.original: Ideo quippe hos potissimum elegi, quoniam de uno Deo qui fecit caelum et terram, quanto melius senserunt, tanto ceteris gloriosiores et inlustriores habentur, in tantum aliis praelati iudicio posterorum, ut, cum Aristoteles, Platonis discipulus, uir excellentis ingenii et eloquio Platoni quidem inpar, sed multos facile superans, cum sectam Peripateticam condidisset, quod deambulans disputare consueuerat, plurimosque discipulos praeclara fama excellens uiuo adhuc praeceptore in suam haeresim congregasset, post mortem uero Platonis Speusippus, sororis eius filius, et Xenocrates, dilectus eius discipulus, in scholam eius, quae Academia uocabatur, eidem successissent adque ob hoc et ipsi et eorum successores Academici appellarentur, recentiores tamen philosophi nobilissimi, quibus Plato sectandus placuit, noluerint se dici Peripateticos aut Academicos, sed Platonicos.
passages.english: For I chose these above all because, the better they thought about the one God who made heaven and earth, the more glorious and illustrious they are held than the rest, so far preferred to others in the judgement of later generations that, although Aristotle, Plato's disciple, a man of outstanding intellect and in eloquence indeed unequal to Plato but easily surpassing many, had founded the Peripatetic school, because he was accustomed to discuss while walking about, and, distinguished by brilliant fame, had gathered very many disciples into his own sect while his teacher was still alive, and although after Plato's death Speusippus, his sister's son, and Xenocrates, his beloved disciple, had succeeded him in his school, which was called the Academy, and for this reason both they and their successors were called Academics, nevertheless the most distinguished more recent philosophers, who chose to follow Plato, did not wish to be called Peripatetics or Academics, but Platonists.

passages.original: Nam et illa ratio Platonis, qua elementa quattuor proportione contexit adque ordinat, ita duobus extremis, igni mobilissimo et terrae inmobili, media duo, aerem et aquam, interserens, ut, quanto est aer aquis et aere ignis, tanto et aquae superiores sint terris, satis nos admonet animalium merita non pro elementorum gradibus aestimare. Et ipse quippe Apuleius cum ceteris terrestre animal hominem dicit, qui tamen longe praeponitur animalibus aquatilibus, cum ipsas aquas terris praeponat Plato: ut intellegant, non eundem ordinem tenendum, cum agitur de meritis animarum, qui uidetur esse ordo in gradibus corporum; sed fieri posse, ut inferius corpus anima melior inhabitet deteriorque superius.
passages.english: For that reasoning of Plato too, by which he links and orders the four elements in proportion, inserting between the two extremes, fire the most mobile and earth the immobile, two means, air and water, so that as air is above water and fire above air, so too water is above earth, sufficiently warns us not to value the merits of living beings according to the ranks of the elements. And Apuleius himself, with the others, calls man a terrestrial living being, who is nevertheless placed far above aquatic beings, although Plato places the waters themselves above the earth: so that they may understand that the same order is not to be kept, when the merits of souls are in question, as appears to be the order in the ranks of bodies; but that it can happen that a better soul inhabits a lower body, and a worse one a higher.

passages.original: Frustra igitur eis Apuleius, et quicumque ita sentiunt, hunc detulit honorem, sic eos in aere medios inter aetherium caelum terramque constituens, ut, quoniam nullus deus miscetur homini, quod Platonem dixisse perhibent, isti ad deos perferant preces hominum et inde ad homines inpetrata quae poscunt. Indignum enim putauerunt qui ista crediderunt misceri homines dis et deos hominibus; dignum autem misceri daemones et dis et hominibus, hinc petita qui adlegent, inde concessa qui adportent;
passages.english: In vain, then, did Apuleius, and whoever thinks thus, confer this honour on them, placing them in the air midway between the ethereal heaven and the earth, so that, since no god mingles with man, which they report Plato said, these may carry the prayers of men to the gods, and from there bring to men what they ask for when it has been granted. For those who believed these things thought it unworthy for men to mingle with gods and gods with men, but worthy for demons to mingle with both gods and men, to present petitions from here and bring back grants from there;

passages.original: Tanta enim homines inpii caecitate in montes quodam modo offendunt resque oculos suos ferientes nolunt uidere. ut non adtendant in omnibus litteris paganorum aut non inueniri aut uix inueniri deos, qui non homines fuerint mortuisque diuini honores delati sint. Omitto, quod Varro dicit omnes ab eis mortuos existimari manes deos et probat per ea sacra, quae omnibus fere mortuis exhibentur, ubi et ludos commemorat funebres, tamquam hoc sit maximum diuinitatis indicium, quod non soleant ludi nisi numinibus celebrari.
passages.english: For impious men, with such great blindness, stumble, as it were, against mountains, and refuse to see things that strike their very eyes, so that they do not notice that in all the literature of the pagans gods are either not found or scarcely found who were not men, and to whom, when dead, divine honours were paid. I pass over the fact that Varro says that all the dead are thought by them to be *manes* gods [spirits of the dead], and proves it by the rites which are performed for nearly all the dead, where he also mentions funeral games, as though this were the greatest sign of divinity, that games are not usually celebrated except for divinities.

passages.original: Duae sunt sententiae philosophorum de his animi motibus, quae Graeci rcdib], nostri autem quidam, sicut Cicero, perturbationes, quidam affectiones uel affectus, quidam uero, sicut iste de Graeco expressius, passiones uocant. Has ergo perturbationes siue affectiones siue passiones quidam philosophi dicunt etiam in sapientem cadere, sed moderatas rationique subiectas, ut eis leges quodam modo, quibus ad necessarium redigantur modum, dominatio mentis inponat.
passages.english: There are two opinions among philosophers about those motions of the mind which the Greeks call *pathē*, while some of our writers, like Cicero, call them disturbances, some affections or feelings, and some, like this author, more literally from the Greek, passions. These disturbances, then, or affections or passions, some philosophers say befall even the wise man, but moderated and subject to reason, so that the mastery of the mind imposes on them laws, as it were, by which they are brought back to the necessary measure.
passages.notes: "rcdib]" is a scanning corruption, evidently of the Greek word πάθη (pathē).

passages.original: Ita mens, ubi fixa est ista sententia, nullas perturbationes, etiamsi accidunt inferioribus animi partibus, in se contra rationem praeualere permittit; quin immo eis ipsa dominatur eisque non consentiendo et potius resistendo regnum uirtutis exercet. Talem describit etiam Vergilius Aenean, ubi ait: Mens inmota manet, lacrimae uoluuntur inanes.
passages.english: So the mind, where this conviction is fixed, allows no disturbances, even if they occur in the lower parts of the soul, to prevail within it against reason; rather, it rules over them itself, and by not consenting to them and instead resisting them it exercises the reign of virtue. Such is the Aeneas that Virgil too describes, where he says: "The mind stays unmoved; the tears roll down in vain."

passages.original: Unde fit consequens, ut haec ipsa non putent uitia, quando sapienti sic accidunt, ut contra uirtutem mentis rationemque nihil possint, et una sit eademque sententia Peripateticorum uel etiam Platonicorum et ipsorum Stoicorum, sed, ut ait Tullius, uerbi controuersia iam diu torqueat homines Graeculos contentionis cupidiores quam ueritatis. Sed adhuc merito quaeri potest, utrum ad uitae praesentis pertineat infirmitatem etiam in quibusque bonis officiis huiusce modi perpeti affectus, sancti uero angeli et sine ira puniant, quos accipiunt aeterna Dei lege puniendos, et miseris sine miseriae conpassione subueniant, et periclitantibus eis, quos diligunt, sine timore opitulentur;
passages.english: From which it follows that they do not consider these things vices when they befall the wise man in such a way that they have no power against the virtue and reason of the mind, and that the opinion of the Peripatetics, or of the Platonists too, and of the Stoics themselves is one and the same, but that, as Tully says, a dispute over words has long tormented little Greeks more eager for contention than for truth. But it can still rightly be asked whether it belongs to the weakness of the present life to undergo feelings of this kind even in all good duties, while the holy angels both punish without anger those whom they receive to be punished by God's eternal law, and help the wretched without fellow-suffering in their wretchedness, and aid without fear those they love when they are in danger;

passages.original: Quod si quisquam dicit, non ex omnium, sed ex malorum daemonum numero esse, quos poetae quorundam hominum os ores et amatores deos non procul a ueritate confingunt (hos enim dixit Apuleius salo mentis per omnes cogitationum aestus fluctuare): quo modo istud intellegere poterimus, quando, cum hoc diceret, non quorundam, id est malorum, sed omnium daemonum medietatem propter aeria corpora inter deos et homines describebat?
passages.english: But if anyone says that it is not from the number of all demons, but of evil ones, that the poets, not far from the truth, invent gods who hate and love certain men (for it was these that Apuleius said toss in the swell of the mind through all the surges of their thoughts): how shall we be able to understand this, since when he said it he was describing the middle position, on account of their aerial bodies, between gods and men not of certain demons, that is, evil ones, but of all demons?
passages.notes: "os ores" read as "osores" (haters).

passages.original: Quaenam tandem istos mediatores falsos adque fallaces quasi capite deorsum nequitia uel poena suspendit, ut inferiorem animalis partem, id est corpus, cum superioribus, superiorem uero, id est animum, cum inferioribus habeant, et cum dis caelestibus in parte seruiente coniuncti, cum hominibus autem terrestribus in parte dominante sint miseri? Corpus quippe seruum est, sicut etiam Sallustius ait: \'Animi imperio, corporis seruitio magis utimur.\' Adiunxit autem ille: \'Alterum nobis cum dis, alterum cum beluis commune est,\' quoniam de hominibus loquebatur, quibus sicut beluis mortale corpus est. Isti autem, quos inter nos et deos mediatores nobis philosophi prouiderunt, possunt quidem dicere de animo et corpore: alterum nobis cum dis, alterum cum hominibus commune est;
passages.english: What wickedness or punishment, pray, has hung these false and deceitful mediators as it were head downward, so that they have the lower part of a living being, that is the body, in common with the higher beings, and the higher part, that is the soul, in common with the lower, and are joined with the heavenly gods in the part that serves, but are wretched with earthly men in the part that rules? For the body is a servant, as Sallust too says: "We use the soul rather for command, the body for service." But he added: "The one we share with the gods, the other with the beasts," since he was speaking of men, who like beasts have a mortal body. But these, whom the philosophers have provided for us as mediators between us and the gods, can indeed say of soul and body: the one we share with the gods, the other with men;
passages.notes: The "one... other" here must be inverted for the demons (body with gods, soul with men), as the following context makes clear.

passages.original: Quod secundum Plotini sententiam minus miseri sint homines in corpore mortali quam daemones in aeterno.
passages.english: That, according to the opinion of Plotinus, men are less wretched in a mortal body than demons in an eternal one.
passages.notes: A chapter heading.

passages.original: Non enim uerum est, quod idem Platonicus ait Platonem dixisse: \'Nullus Deus miscetur homini*; et hoc praecipuum eorum sublimitatis ait esse specimen, quod nulla adtrectatione hominum contaminantur. Ergo daemones contaminari fatetur, et ideo eos, a quibus contaminantur, mundare non possunt omnesque inmundi pariter fiunt, et daemones contrectatione hominum et homines cultu daemonum.
passages.english: For it is not true, as the same Platonist says that Plato said: 'No god mingles with man'; and he says that this is the chief mark of their sublimity, that they are not contaminated by any contact with men. So he admits that the demons are contaminated, and therefore they cannot cleanse those by whom they are contaminated, and all alike become unclean, the demons through contact with men and men through the worship of demons.
passages.notes: 'The same Platonist' is Apuleius, judging by the surrounding argument. The asterisk after 'homini' is a stray mark standing for a closing quotation mark.

passages.original: Miror autem plurimum tam doctos homines, qui cuncta corporalia et sensibilia prae incorporalibus et intellegibilibus postponenda iudicauerunt, cum agitur de beata uita, corporalium contrectationum facere mentionem. Ubi est illud Plotini, ubi ait: Fugiendum est igitur ad carissimam patriam, et ibi pater, et ibi omnia. Quae igitur, inquit, classis aut fuga? Similem Deo fieri.\' Si ergo deo quanto similior, tanto fit quisque propinquior, nulla est ab illo alia longinquitas quam eius dissimilitudo.
passages.english: I am greatly astonished, however, that such learned men, who judged that all corporeal and sensible things are to be ranked below incorporeal and intelligible ones, should make mention of bodily contacts when the happy life is in question. Where is that saying of Plotinus, where he says: 'We must flee, then, to our dearest fatherland, and there is the Father, and there is everything. What, then,' he says, 'is the fleet or the flight? To become like God.' If, then, the more like God anyone becomes, the nearer he comes to him, there is no other distance from him than unlikeness to him.
passages.notes: 'Classis' (fleet) is the reading given; the quotation echoes the image of a sea voyage home.

passages.original: Hos si Platonici malunt deos quam daemones dicere eisque adnumerare, quos a summo Deo conditos deos scribit eorum auctor et magister Plato: dicant quod uolunt; non enim cum eis de uerborum controuersia laborandum est. Si enim sic inmortales, ut tamen a summo Deo factos, et si non per se ipsos, sed ei, a quo facti sunt, adhaerendo beatos esse dicunt: hoc dicunt quod dicimus, quolibet eos nomine appellent.
passages.english: If the Platonists prefer to call these gods rather than demons, and to count them among those whom their founder and teacher Plato writes were made gods by the supreme God, let them say what they like; for we need not labour with them over a dispute about words. For if they say that they are immortal in such a way as nevertheless to have been made by the supreme God, and that they are happy not through themselves but by cleaving to him by whom they were made, they say what we say, by whatever name they call them.

passages.original: Viderunt enim suisque litteris multis modis copiosissime mandauerunt hinc illos, unde et nos, fieri beatos, obiecto quodam lumine intellegibili. quod Deus est illis et aliud est quam illi, a quo inlustrantur, ut clareant adque eius participatione perfecti beatique subsistant. Saepe multumque Plotinus adserit sensum Platonis explanans, ne illam quidem, quam credunt esse uniuersitatis animam, aliunde beatam esse quam nostram, idque esse lumen quod ipsa non est, sed a quo creata est et quo intellegibiliter inluminante intellegibiliter lucet.
passages.english: For they saw, and in their writings set down very abundantly and in many ways, that those [beings] are made happy from the same source as we are: by a certain intelligible light shining upon them, which is God to them and is something other than they are. They are illuminated by it so that they may shine, and by participation in it they subsist perfect and happy. Plotinus, explaining the meaning of Plato, often and at length asserts that not even that [soul] which they believe to be the soul of the universe is happy from any source other than our soul is. He asserts that this [source] is a light which that soul itself is not, but by which it was created, and by whose intelligible illumination it shines intelligibly.
passages.notes: The punctuation before 'quod Deus est' is odd in the edition; the clause is taken as a relative clause depending on 'lumine'.

passages.original: Et quod ei uidetur herbis et lapidibus et animantibus et sonis certis quibusdam ac uocibus et figurationibus adque figmentis, quibusdam etiam obseruatis in caeli conuersione motibus siderum fabricari in terra ab hominibus potestates idoneas uariis effectibus exsequendis, totum hoc ad eosdem ipsos daemones pertinet ludificatores animarum sibimet subditarum et uoluptaria sibi ludibria de hominum erroribus exhibentes. Aut ergo re uera dubitans et inquirens ista Porphyrius ea tamen commemorat, quibus conuincantur et redarguantur, nec ad eas potestates, quae nobis ad beatam uitam capessendam fauent, sed ad deceptores daemones pertinere monstrentur; aut, ut meliora de philosopho suspicemur, eo modo uoluit hominem Aegyptium talibus erroribus deditum et aliqua magna se scire opinantem non superba quasi auctoritate doctoris offendere, nec aperte aduersantis altercatione turbare, sed quasi quaerentis et discere cupientis humilitate ad ea cogitanda conuertere et quam sint contemnenda uel etiam deuitanda monstrare.
passages.english: And as for his view that powers suited to bringing about various effects are fashioned on earth by men out of herbs and stones and animals, and certain particular sounds and words, and shapes and figures, and also certain movements of the stars observed in the revolution of the sky: all this belongs to those same demons. They make sport of the souls subject to them, and provide themselves with pleasurable amusement out of the errors of men. Either, then, Porphyry really doubts and inquires into these things, and yet mentions the things by which they may be refuted and disproved, and shown to belong not to the powers that help us to attain the happy life but to deceiving demons. Or else, to think better of the philosopher, he wished in this way to deal with an Egyptian given to such errors and thinking that he knew some great things. He wished not to offend him by the proud authority, as it were, of a teacher, nor to unsettle him by the wrangling of an open opponent. Instead, with the humility of one who seeks and wishes to learn, he wished to turn him to thinking about these things and to show how much they are to be despised or even avoided.

passages.original: ita sane ut etiam illo tempore, quo uisibilia promittebantur diuinitus praemia, unus tamen colendus commendaretur Deus, ne mens humana uel pro ipsis terrenis uitae transitoriae beneficiis cuiquam nisi uero animae creatori et domino subderetur. Omnia quippe, quae praestare hominibus uel angeli uel homines possunt, in unius esse Omnipotentis potestate quisquis diffitetur, insanit. De prouidentia certe Plotinus Platonicus disputat eamque a summo Deo, cuius est intellegibilis adque ineffabilis pulchritudo, usque ad haec terrena et ima pertingere flosculorum adque foliorum pulchritudine conprobat; quae omnia quasi abiecta et uelocissime pereuntia decentissimos formarum suarum numeros habere non posse confirmat, nisi inde formentur, ubi forma intellegibilis et incommutabilis simul habens omnia perseuerat.
passages.english: [The training of the human race advanced] in such a way that even at that time, when visible rewards were promised by God, one God alone was nevertheless commended to be worshipped. This was so that the human mind should not be made subject to anyone except the true creator and lord of the soul, even for the sake of the earthly benefits of this passing life. For whoever denies that everything which either angels or men can bestow on men lies in the power of the one Almighty is mad. The Platonist Plotinus certainly discusses providence. He proves from the beauty of little flowers and leaves that it reaches from the supreme God, whose beauty is intelligible and ineffable, all the way down to these earthly and lowest things. He affirms that all these things, though cast down as it were and perishing very swiftly, could not have the most fitting proportions of their forms unless they were formed from that place where the intelligible and unchangeable form endures, holding all things at once.
passages.notes: The passage begins in mid-sentence, continuing from the context before. The bracketed opening supplies the sense of that context.

passages.original: Nam Paulus et Barnabas in Lycaonia facto quodam miraculo sanitatis putati sunt di, eisque Lycaonii uictimas immolare uoluerunt; quod a se humili pietate remouentes eis in quem crederent adnuntiauerunt Deum. Nec ob aliud fallaces illi superbe sibi hoc exigunt, nisi quia uero Deo deberi sciunt. Non enim re uera, ut ait Porphyrius et nonnulli putant, cadauerinis nidoribus, sed diuinis honoribus gaudent. Copiam uero nidorum magnam habent undique, et si amplius uellent, ipsi sibi poterant exhibere. Qui ergo diuinitatem sibi adrogant spiritus, non cuiuslibet corporis fumo, sed supplicantis animo delectantur, cui decepto subiectoque dominentur, intercludentes iter ad Deum uerum, ne sit homo illius sacrificium, dum sacrificatur cuipiam praeter illum.
passages.english: For Paul and Barnabas, when a certain miracle of healing had been done in Lycaonia, were thought to be gods, and the Lycaonians wanted to sacrifice victims to them. Turning this away from themselves with humble piety, they proclaimed to them the God in whom they should believe. Those deceivers proudly demand this for themselves for no other reason than that they know it is owed to the true God. For in truth, as Porphyry says and some think, it is not the reek of carcasses they delight in but divine honours. They have a great abundance of smells from every side, and if they wanted more they could provide it for themselves. So the spirits who claim divinity for themselves delight not in the smoke of any body but in the mind of the suppliant. Once that mind is deceived and subjected, they may rule over it, blocking the way to the true God, so that man may not be his sacrifice while he is sacrificed to someone other than him.
passages.notes: 'Non enim re uera, ut ait Porphyrius' is ambiguous: either Porphyry and others think the demons delight in the reek, which Augustine denies, or the phrase 'as Porphyry says' attaches to the denial. It is rendered literally.

passages.original: Sed a contrario martyres nostri heroes nuncuparentur, si, ut dixi, usus ecclesiastici sermonis admitteret, non quo eis esset cum daemonibus in aere societas, sed quod eosdem daemones, id est aerias uincerent potestates et in eis ipsam, quidquid putatur significare, Iunonem, quae non usquequaque inconuenienter a poetis inducitur inimica uirtutibus et caelum petentibus uiris fortibus inuida. Sed . rursus ei succumbit infeliciter ceditque Vergilius, ut, cum aput eum illa dicat:Vincor ab Aenea, ipsum Aenean admoneat Helenus quasi consilio religioso et dicat: Iunoni cane nota libens, dominamque potentem Supplicibus supera donis. Ex qua opinione Porphyrius, quamuis non ex sua sententia, sed ex aliorum, dicit bonum deum uel genium non uenire in hominem, nisi malus fuerit ante placatus;
passages.english: But our martyrs would be called heroes in the opposite sense, if, as I said, the usage of church language allowed it. It would not be because they had fellowship with the demons in the air. It would be because they conquer those same demons, that is, the powers of the air, and among them Juno herself, whatever she is thought to signify. The poets, not altogether unfittingly, present her as hostile to virtues and envious of brave men seeking heaven. But Virgil in turn unhappily gives in and yields to her. In his poem she says, 'I am conquered by Aeneas,' and yet Helenus advises Aeneas himself, as if with religious counsel, saying: 'Willingly chant vows to Juno, and overcome the mighty mistress with suppliant gifts.' From this opinion Porphyry, though not in his own view but in that of others, says that a good god or genius does not come to a man unless the evil one has first been appeased;
passages.notes: A stray period after 'Sed' is ignored. The passage ends mid-sentence.

passages.original: Dicit etiam Porphyrius diuinis oraculis fuisse responsum nos non purgari lunae teletis adque solis, ut hinc ostenderetur nullorum deorum teletis hominem posse purgari. Cuius enim teletae purgant, si lunae solisque non purgant, quos inter caelestes deos praecipuos habent?
passages.english: Porphyry also says that the divine oracles replied that we are not purified by the *teletae* [initiatory rites] of the moon and the sun, so that it might be shown from this that a man cannot be purified by the *teletae* of any gods. For whose *teletae* purify, if those of the moon and sun do not, whom they hold to be chief among the celestial gods?
passages.notes: *Teletae* is a Greek term for initiation rites or mysteries.

passages.original: Dicit enim Deum Patrem et Deum Filium, quem Graece appellat paternum intellectum uel paternam mentem; de Spiritu autem sancto aut nihil aut non aperte aliquid dicit; quamuis quem alium dicat horum medium, non intellego. Si enim tertiam, sicut Plotinus, ubi de tribus principalibus substantiis disputat, animae naturam etiam iste uellet intellegi, non utique diceret horum medium, id est Patris et Filii medium. Postponit quippe Plotinus animae naturam paterno intellectui;
passages.english: For he speaks of God the Father and God the Son, whom he calls in Greek the paternal intellect or paternal mind; but of the Holy Spirit he says either nothing or nothing openly; although I do not understand whom else he means by the one "midway between these." For if he, like Plotinus where he discusses the three principal substances, wished the nature of the soul to be understood as the third, he would surely not say "midway between these," that is, midway between the Father and the Son. For Plotinus places the nature of the soul after the paternal intellect;

passages.original: non enim mala disceret, si non faceret), in eo tamen aliorum Platonicorum opinionem et non in re parua emendauit, quod mundatam ab omnibus malis animam et cum Patre constitutam numquam iam mala mundi huius passuram esse confessus est. Qua sententia profecto abstulit, quod esse Platonicum maxime perhibetur, ut mortuos ex uiuis, ita uiuos ex mertuis semper fieri; falsumque esse ostendit, quod Platonice uidetur dixisse Vergilius, in campos Elysios purgatas animas missas (quo nomine tamquam per fabulam uidentur significari gaudia beatorum) ad fluuium Letheum euocari, hoc est ad obliuionem praeteritorum: Scilicet inmemores supera ut conuexa reuisant Rursus et incipiant in corpora uelle reuerti.
passages.english: for it would not learn evils if it did not do them), yet in this he corrected the opinion of the other Platonists, and on no small matter, that he acknowledged that the soul cleansed of all evils and established with the Father will never again suffer the evils of this world. By this view he certainly removed what is said to be most characteristically Platonic, that just as the dead come from the living, so the living always come from the dead; and he showed to be false what Virgil seems to have said in Platonic fashion, that souls sent, once purified, into the Elysian fields (by which name, as if through a fable, the joys of the blessed seem to be signified) are called to the river Lethe, that is, to forgetfulness of the past: "So that, forgetful, they may see again the vault above and begin once more to wish to return into bodies."
passages.notes: "mertuis" read as "mortuis".

passages.original: Non enim beata erit nisi secura; ut autem secura sit, falso putabit semper se beatam fore, quoniam aliquando erit et misera. Cui ergo gaudendi causa falsitas erit, quo modo de ueritate gaudebit? Vidit hoc Porphyrius purgatamque animam ob hoc reuerti dixit ad Patrem, ne aliquando iam malorum polluta contagione teneatur. Falso igitur a quibusdam est Platonicis creditus quasi necessarius orbis ille ab eisdem abeundi et ad eadem reuertendi. Quod etiamsi uerum esset, quid hoc scire prodesset, nisi forte inde se nobis auderent praeferre Platonici, quia id nos in hac uita iam nesciremus, quod ipsi in alia meliore uita purgatissimi et sapientissimi fuerant nescituri et falsum credendo beati futuri?
passages.english: For it will not be blessed unless it is secure; but in order to be secure, it will falsely think that it will always be blessed, since at some time it will also be wretched. How then will it rejoice in the truth, when falsehood will be its cause of rejoicing? Porphyry saw this, and said that the purified soul returns to the Father for this reason, that it may never again be held polluted by the contagion of evils. Falsely, therefore, was that cycle of departing from the same things and returning to the same things believed by some Platonists to be, as it were, necessary. Even if this were true, what would it profit to know it, unless perhaps the Platonists would dare to set themselves above us on this ground, that we in this life would already not know what they themselves, most purified and most wise, were going not to know in another, better life, and were going to be blessed by believing a falsehood?

passages.original: Ut enim hoc Platonici nollent credere, hanc utique causam idoneam sibi uidebantur adferre, quia, nisi quod semper antea fuisset, sempiternum deinceps esse non posset; quamquam et de mundo et de his, quos in mundo deos a Deo factos scribit Plato, apertissime dicat eos esse coepisse et habere initium, finem tamen non habituros, sed per conditoris potentissimam uoluntatem in aeternum mansuros esse perhibeat. Verum id quo modo intellegant inuenerunt, non esse hoc uidelicet temporis, sed substitutionis initium.
passages.english: For in refusing to believe this, the Platonists seemed to themselves to offer at least this suitable reason: that unless something had always existed before, it could not be everlasting thereafter; although concerning both the world and those whom Plato writes were made gods in the world by God, he says most plainly that they began to exist and have a beginning, yet he declares that they will not have an end, but will remain forever through the most powerful will of their maker. But they have found a way to understand this, namely that this is a beginning not of time but of dependence.
passages.notes: "substitutionis" is unusual; sense apparently 'of being placed under/dependent on a cause', i.e. causal rather than temporal beginning.

passages.original: exceptis ipsius Saluatoris propriis singularibusque miraculis, maxime natiuitatis et resurrectionis, quorum in uno maternae uirginitatis tantummodo sacramentum, in altero autem etiam eorum, qui in fine resurrecturi sunt, demonstrauit exemplum. Haec uia totum hominem mundat et inmortalitati mortalem ex omnibus quibus constat partibus praeparat. Ut enim non alia purgatio ei parti quaereretur, quam uocat intellectualem Porphyrius, alia ei, quam uocat spiritalem, aliaque ipsi corpori: propterea totum suscepit ueracissimus potentissimusque mundator adque saluator. Praeter hanc uiam, quae, partim cum haec futura praenuntiantur, partim cum facta nuntiantur, numquam generi humano defuit, nemo liberatus est, nemo liberatur, nemo liberabitur.
passages.english: apart from the Saviour's own proper and singular miracles, above all of his birth and resurrection, in the one of which he showed only the mystery of his mother's virginity, but in the other also an example for those who will rise at the end. This way cleanses the whole man and prepares the mortal for immortality in all the parts of which he consists. For so that one purification should not be sought for the part which Porphyry calls intellectual, another for that which he calls spiritual, and another for the body itself, for this reason the most truthful and most powerful cleanser and saviour took up the whole [man]. Apart from this way, which has never been lacking to the human race, partly when these things are foretold as future, partly when they are announced as done, no one has been set free, no one is set free, no one will be set free.

passages.original: si per quid fecerit: Dixit: Fiat, et facta est; si quare fecerit: Quia bona est. Nec auctor est excellentior Deo, nec ars efficacior Dei uerbo, nec causa melior quam ut bonum crearetur a [Deo] bono. Hanc etiam Plato causam condendi mundi iustissimam dicit, ut a bono Deo bona opera fierent; siue ista legerit, siue ab his qui legerant forte cognouerit; siue acerrimo ingenio inuisibilia Dei per ea, quae facta sunt, intellecta conspexerit, siue ab his qui ista conspexerant et ipse didicerit.
passages.english: if [we ask] through what he made it: "He said, 'Let it be,' and it was made"; if why he made it: "Because it is good." There is no author more excellent than God, no art more effective than the Word of God, no cause better than that something good should be created by a good God. Plato too says this is the most just cause of founding the world, that good works should be made by a good God; whether he read these things, or perhaps learned them from those who had read them, or whether with his most penetrating intellect he perceived the invisible things of God, understood through the things that have been made, or he too learned from those who had perceived these things.

passages.original: Omittamus igitur coniecturas hominum nescientium quid loquantur de natura uel institutione generis humani. Alii namque, sicut de ipso mundo crediderunt, semper fuisse homines opinantur. Unde et ait Apuleius, cum hoc animantium genus describeret: \'Singillatim mortales, cuncti tamen uniuerso genere perpetui.\' Et cum illis dictum fuerit, si semper fuit humanum genus, quonam modo uerum eorum loquatur historia narrans qui fuerint quarumque rerum inuentores, qui primi liberalium disciplinarum aliarumque artium institutores.
passages.english: Let us therefore set aside the conjectures of men who do not know what they are saying about the nature or establishment of the human race. For some, as they believed about the world itself, hold that men have always existed. Hence Apuleius too says, when describing this kind of living creature: "Individually mortal, yet all together perpetual as a whole kind." And when it has been said to them: if the human race has always existed, how does their history speak truly in narrating who were the inventors of what things, who the first founders of the liberal disciplines and other arts,
passages.notes: Sentence continues into the following context.

passages.original: Quod autem respondimus, cum de mundi origine quaestio uerteretur, eis, qui nolunt credere non eum semper fuisse, sed esse coepisse, sicut etiam Plato apertissime confitetur, quamuis a nonnullis contra quam loquitur sensisse credatur: hoc etiam de prima hominis conditione responderim, propter eos, qui similiter mouentur, quur homo per innumerabilia adque infinita retro tempora creatus non sit tamque sero sit creatus, ut minus quam sex milia sint annorum, ex quo esse coepisse in sacris litteris inuenitur.
passages.english: But what we answered, when the question turned on the origin of the world, to those who will not believe that it did not always exist but began to exist, as even Plato most plainly admits, although by some he is believed to have held the opposite of what he says: this I would also answer concerning the first creation of man, on account of those who are similarly troubled as to why man was not created during innumerable and infinite past ages, and was created so late that it is less than six thousand years since he is found in the sacred writings to have begun to exist.

passages.original: Ita sane Plato minores et a summo Deo factos deos effectores esse uoluit animalium ceterorum, ut inmortalem partem ab ipso sumerent, ipsi uero mortalem adtexerent. Proinde animarum nostrarum eos creatores noluit esse, sed corporum. Unde quoniam Porphyrius propter animae purgationem dicit corpus omne fugiendum simulque cum suo Platone aliisque Platonicis sentit eos, qui inmoderate adque inhoneste uixerint, propter luendas poenas ad corpora redire mortalia, Plato quidem etiam bestiarum, Porphyrius tantummodo ad hominum: sequitur eos, ut dicant deos istos, quos a nobis uolunt quasi parentes et conditores nostros coli, nihil esse aliud quam fabros conpedum carcerumue nostrorum, nec institutores, sed inclusores adligatoresque nostros ergastulis aerumnosis et grauissimis uinculis.
passages.english: Plato indeed held that the lesser gods, made by the supreme God, were the makers of the other living creatures in such a way that they received the immortal part from him, and themselves wove on the mortal part. Accordingly he did not want them to be the creators of our souls, but of our bodies. Hence, since Porphyry says that for the purification of the soul every body must be fled, and at the same time holds with his Plato and other Platonists that those who have lived immoderately and dishonourably return to mortal bodies to pay penalties (Plato indeed even to those of beasts, Porphyry only to those of men), it follows for them that they must say these gods, whom they want us to worship as our parents and founders, are nothing other than the smiths of our fetters or prisons, not our establishers but our jailers, who shut us up and bind us in wretched workhouses and most heavy chains.

passages.original: Sed cum apertissime Plato deos a summo Deo factos habere inmortalia corpora praedicet eisque ipsum Deum, a quo facti sunt, inducat pro magno beneficio pollicentem, quod in aeternum cum suis corporibus permanebunt nec ab eis ulla morte soluentur: quid est quod isti ad exagitandam Christianam fidem fingunt se nescire quod sciunt, aut etiam sibi repugnantes aduersum se ipsos malunt dicere, dum nobis non desinant contradicere? Nempe Platonis haec uerba sunt, sicut ea Cicero in Latinum uertit, quibus inducit summum deum deos quos fecit adloquentem ac dicentem: Vos, qui deorum satu orti estis, adtendite: quorum operum ego parens effectorque sum, haec sunt indissolubilia me inuito, quamquam omne conligatum solui potest; sed haudquaquam bonum est ratione uinctum uelle dissoluere. Sed quoniam estis orti, inmortales uos quidem esse et indissolubiles non potestis;
passages.english: But since Plato most plainly proclaims that the gods made by the supreme God have immortal bodies, and introduces that very God by whom they were made promising them as a great benefit that they will remain forever with their bodies and will not be separated from them by any death: why is it that these men, to harass the Christian faith, pretend not to know what they know, or even, contradicting themselves, prefer to speak against themselves so long as they do not cease to contradict us? For these are Plato's words, as Cicero translated them into Latin, in which he introduces the supreme god addressing the gods he made and saying: "You who have sprung from the seed of gods, attend: of the works of which I am parent and maker, these are indissoluble against my will, although everything that is bound together can be undone; but it is by no means good to wish to undo what has been bound by reason. But since you have come into being, you cannot indeed be immortal and indissoluble;

passages.original: ne utiquam tamen dissoluemini, neque uos ulla mortis fata periment, nec erunt ualentiora quam consilium meum, quod maius est uinculum ad perpetuitatem uestram, quam illa quibus estis [tum, cum gignebamini,] conligati). Ecce deos Plato dicit et corporis animaeque conligatione mortales, et tamen inmortales dei a quo facti sunt uoluntate adque consilio. Si ergo animae poena est in qualicumque corpore conligari, quid est quod eos adloquens deus tamquam sollicitos, ne forte moriantur, id est dissoluantur a corpore, de sua facit inmortalitate securos;
passages.english: yet you will by no means be dissolved, nor will any fates of death destroy you, nor will they be stronger than my purpose, which is a greater bond for your perpetuity than those with which you were bound [then, when you were being begotten]." Behold, Plato says the gods are mortal by the binding together of body and soul, and yet immortal by the will and purpose of the god by whom they were made. If then it is a punishment for the soul to be bound in any body whatever, why is it that the god, addressing them as if anxious lest they should die, that is, be separated from the body, makes them secure of their immortality;
passages.notes: The bracketed words are marked by the edition as doubtful/interpolated.

passages.original: Et hoc quidem utrum Plato uerum de sideribus dicat, alia quaestio est. Neque enim ei continuo concedendum est globos istos luminum siue orbiculos luce corporea super terras seu die seu nocte fulgentes suis quibusdam propriis animis uiuere eisque intellectualibus et beatis, quod etiam de ipso uniuerso mundo, tamquam uno animali maximo, quo cuncta cetera continerentur animalia, instanter adfirmat.
passages.english: Whether Plato speaks the truth about the stars in this, however, is another question. For we need not at once concede to him that those globes of light, or little orbs, shining with bodily light over the earth by day or by night, live by certain souls of their own, and these intellectual and blessed, which he also insistently affirms of the whole universe itself, as of one very great living being in which all other living beings are contained.

passages.original: Si quis hoc etiam de igne similiter adfirmet et dicat reddenda esse uniuerso igni corpora, quae inde sumta sunt, ut caelestia fierent animalia: nonne inmortalitas, quam talibus dis, uelut deo summo loquente, promisit Plato, tamquam uiolentia disputationis huius intercidet? An ibi propterea non fit, quia Deus non uult, cuius uoluntatem, ut ait Plato, nulla uis uincit? Quid ergo prohibet, ut hoc etiam de terrestribus corporibus Deus possit efficere, quandoquidem, ut nec ea quae orta sunt occidant nec ea quae sunt uincta soluantur nec ea quae sunt ex elementis sumta reddantur adque ut animae in corporibus constitutae nec umquam ea deserant et cum eis inmortalitate ac sempiterna beatitudine perfruantur, posse Deum facere confitetur Plato?
passages.english: If someone were likewise to affirm this of fire too, and say that the bodies taken from it to make the heavenly living beings must be given back to the whole of fire, would not the immortality which Plato promised to such gods, as though the highest god were speaking, perish as it were under the force of this argument? Or does it not happen there for this reason, that God does not will it, whose will, as Plato says, no force overcomes? What then prevents God from being able to bring this about with earthly bodies as well, since Plato admits that God can bring it about that things which have come into being do not perish, that things which are bound together are not loosed, that things taken from the elements are not given back, and that souls set in bodies never desert them and enjoy with them immortality and everlasting blessedness?

passages.original: Si enim ars humana efficit, ut ex metallis, quae in aquis posita continuo submerguntur, quibusdam modis uasa fabricata etiam natare possint: quanto credibilius et efficacius occultus aliquis modus operationis Dei, cuius omnipotentissima uoluntate Plato dicit nec orta interire nec conligata posse dissolui, cum multo mirabilius incorporea corporeis quam quaecumque corpora quibuscumque corporibus copulentur, potest molibus praestare terrenis, ut nullo in ima pondere deprimantur, ipsisque animis perfectissime beatis, ut quamuis terrena, tamen incorruptibilia iam corpora ubi uolunt ponant et quo uolunt agant, situ motuque facillimo!
passages.english: For if human skill brings it about that, from metals which sink at once when placed in water, vessels fashioned in certain ways can even float, how much more credibly and effectively can some hidden mode of God's working, by whose most omnipotent will, Plato says, things that have come into being cannot perish nor things bound together be loosed (although incorporeal things are joined to corporeal ones far more wonderfully than any bodies whatever to any other bodies), grant to earthly masses that they are pressed down to the depths by no weight, and grant to the souls themselves, perfectly blessed, that they may place their bodies, earthly yet now incorruptible, where they will and move them whither they will, with the easiest positioning and motion!

passages.original: Neque enim quisquam audebit illorum sapientes homines, siue morituros siue iam mortuos, id est aut carentes corporibus aut corpora relicturos, dis inmortalibus anteponere. quibus Deus summus aput Platonem munus ingens, indissolubilem scilicet uitam, id est aeternum cum suis corporibus consortium, pollicetur. Optime autem cum hominibus agi arbitratur idem Plato, si tamen hanc uitam pie iusteque peregerint, ut a suis corporibus separati in ipsorum deorum, qui sua corpora numquam deserunt, recipiantur sinum, . Scilicet inmemores supera ut conuexa reuisant Rursus et incipiant in corpora uelle reuerti;
passages.english: For none of them will dare to rank wise men, whether about to die or already dead, that is, either lacking bodies or about to leave them, above the immortal gods, to whom the highest God in Plato promises an immense gift, namely indissoluble life, that is, eternal partnership with their bodies. Yet the same Plato thinks it goes best with men, provided they have lived this life piously and justly, that, separated from their bodies, they are received into the bosom of those very gods who never desert their bodies, "so that, forgetful, they may revisit the vault above and begin again to wish to return into bodies";
passages.notes: The stray comma before the quotation suggests a gap or misprint; the verse is Virgil, Aeneid 6.750–51.

passages.original: Proinde nunc sanctorum animae defunctorum ideo non habent grauem mortem, qua separatae sunt a corporibus suis, quia caro eorum requiescit in spe. quaslibet sine ullo iam sensu contumelias accepisse uideatur. Non enim, sicut Platoni uisum est, corpora obliuione desiderant, sed potius, quia meminerunt quid sibi ab eo sit promissum, qui neminem fallit, qui eis etiam de capillorum suorum integritate securitatem dedit, resurrectionem corporum, in quibus multa dura perpessi sunt, nihil in eis ulterius tale sensuri desiderabiliter et patienter expectant.
passages.english: Accordingly the souls of the departed saints do not now find heavy the death by which they have been separated from their bodies, because their flesh rests in hope, whatever insults it may seem to have received when it no longer has any feeling. For they do not, as Plato thought, desire bodies through forgetfulness; rather, because they remember what has been promised them by him who deceives no one, who gave them assurance even of the safety of their hairs, they wait longingly and patiently for the resurrection of the bodies in which they endured many hard things, and in which they will never again feel anything of the kind.
passages.notes: "quaslibet ... uideatur" seems to lack its antecedent (perhaps a phrase about the flesh has dropped out); translated as referring to the flesh.

passages.original: uerum tamen ex terrenis artubus moribundisque membris sic adfici animas opinantur, ut hinc eis sint morbi cupiditatum et timorum et laetitiae siue tristitiae; quibus quattuor uel perturbationibus, ut Cicero appellat, uel passionibus, ut plerique uerbum e uerbo Graeco exprimunt, omnis humanorum morum uitiositas continetur. Quod si ita est, quid est quod Aeneas aput Vergilium, cum audisset a patre aput inferos animas rursus ad corpora redituras, hanc opinionem miratur exclamans: O pater, anne aliquas ad caelum hinc ire putandum est Sublimes animas iterumque ad tarda reuerti Corpora?
passages.english: but they think that souls are so affected by earthly limbs and dying members that from these come their diseases of desires and fears, and of joy or sadness; in which four, whether disturbances, as Cicero calls them, or passions, as most render the Greek word word for word, all the viciousness of human conduct is contained. If this is so, why is it that Aeneas in Virgil, when he heard from his father in the underworld that souls would return again to bodies, marvels at this opinion, exclaiming: "O father, must we think that some souls go hence up to the sky, lofty, and return again to sluggish bodies?"

passages.original: Hoc tamen loquendi obtinuit consuetudo, ut, si cupi- ■ ditas uel concupiscentia dicatur nec addatur cuius rei sit, non nisi in malo possit intellegi. Laetitia in bono est: Laetamini in Domino et exultate iusti; et: Dedisti laetitiam in cor meum; et: Adinplebis me laetitia cum uultu tuo. Timor in bono est aput apostolum, ubi ait: Cum timore et tremore uestram ipsorum salutem operamini; et: Noli altum sapere, sed time; et: Timeo autem, ne, sicut serpens Euam seduxit astutia sua. sic et uestrae mentes corrumpantur a castitate, quae est in Christo. De tristitia uero, quam Cicero magis aegritudinem appellat, dolorem autem Vergilius, ubi ait: (dolent gaudentque\', (sed ideo malui tristitiam dicere, quia aegritudo uel dolor usitatius in corporibus dicitur) scrupulosior quaestio est, utrum inueniri possit in bono.
passages.english: Yet the custom of speech has prevailed that if "desire" (cupiditas) or "concupiscence" is spoken of without adding what it is for, it can be understood only in a bad sense. Joy is in a good sense: "Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous"; and: "You have put joy in my heart"; and: "You will fill me with joy with your countenance." Fear is in a good sense in the apostle, where he says: "Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling"; and: "Do not be high-minded, but fear"; and: "But I fear lest, as the serpent seduced Eve by his cunning, so your minds too may be corrupted from the chastity that is in Christ." But concerning sadness, which Cicero rather calls sickness (aegritudo), and Virgil pain, where he says "they grieve and rejoice" (but I preferred to say sadness because sickness or pain is more usually said of bodies), it is a more delicate question whether it can be found in a good sense.

passages.original: Sic ergo illi loquuntur, ut uelle gaudere cauere negent nisi sapientem; stultum autem non nisi cupere laetari, metuere contristari; et illas tres esse constantias, has autem quattuor perturbationes secundum Ciceronem, secundum autem plurimos passiones. Graece autem illae tres, sicut dixi, appellantur eorcatetai; istae autem quattuor πάθη. Haec locutio utrum scripturis sanctis congruat, cum quaererem quantum potui diligenter, illud inueni quod ait propheta: Non est gaudere inpiis, dicit Dominus; tamquam inpii laetari possint potius quam gaudere de malis, quia gaudium proprie bonorum et piorum est. Item illud in euangelio: Quaecumque uultis ut faciant uobis homines, haec et uos facite illis, ita dictum uidetur, tamquam nemo possit aliquid male uel turpiter uelle, sed cupere. Denique propter consuetudinem locutionis nonnulli interpretes addiderunt \'bona* et ita interpretati sunt: \'Quaecumque uultis ut faciant uobis homines bona.\' Cauendum enim putauerunt, ne quisquam inhonesta uelit sibi fieri ab hominibus, ut de turpioribus taceam, certe luxuriosa conuiuia, in quibus se, si et ipse illis faciat, hoc praeceptum existimet iupleturum.
passages.english: So they speak in such a way as to deny that anyone but the wise man wills, rejoices, and is cautious, while the fool only desires, is glad, fears, and is saddened; and [they say] the former three are constancies, the latter four disturbances according to Cicero, but according to most people passions. In Greek, as I said, those three are called eupatheiai, and these four pathē. Whether this usage agrees with holy scripture, when I inquired as carefully as I could, I found this saying of the prophet: "There is no rejoicing for the impious, says the Lord"; as though the impious can be glad rather than rejoice over evil things, since rejoicing properly belongs to the good and pious. Likewise that saying in the gospel, "Whatever you will that men should do to you, do so also to them," seems to be said as though no one can will anything evilly or shamefully, but only desire it. Finally, because of the custom of speech, some translators added "good things" and translated thus: "Whatever good things you will that men should do to you." For they thought one must beware lest anyone should will dishonourable things to be done to him by men, certainly (to say nothing of fouler things) luxurious banquets, in which he might think he would fulfil this precept if he too provided them for others.
passages.notes: "eorcatetai" is a scanning garble of Greek eupatheiai; "iupleturum" read as impleturum.

passages.original: Quid autem magnum in caritatis laudibus dixisset apostolus, quod non gaudeat super iniquitate, nisi quia ita malignitas gaudet? Et aput auctores saecularium litterarum talis istorum uerborum indifferentia reperitur. Ait enim Cicero orator amplissimus: (Cupio, patres conscripti, me esse clementem.) Quia id uerbum in bono posuit. quis tam peruerse doctus existat, qui non eum \'Cupio\', sed \'Volo* potius dicere debuisse contendat? Porro aput Terentium flagitiosus adulescens insana flagrans cupidine:.
passages.english: What great thing would the apostle have said in praise of love, that it does not rejoice over iniquity, unless malice does so rejoice? And among authors of secular literature such indifference in the use of these words is found. For Cicero, a most distinguished orator, says: "I desire, conscript fathers, to be merciful." Since he used that word in a good sense, who would be so perversely learned as to contend that he ought to have said not "I desire" but rather "I will"? Again, in Terence a profligate youth, burning with mad desire, [says]:
passages.notes: The passage breaks off before the Terence quotation, which follows in the context.

passages.original: Et si ideo mori uelit, non quo nolit uiuere, sed ut post mortem melius uiuat: nondum ergo ut uult uiuit, sed cum ad id quod uult moriendo peruenerit. Verum ecce uiuat ut uult, quoniam sibi extorsit sibique imperauit non uelle quod non potest, adque hoc uelle quod potest, sicut ait Terentius: Quoniam non potest id fieri quod uis, Id uelis quod possis: num ideo beatus est, quia patienter miser est? Beata quippe uita si non amatur, non habetur. Porro si amatur et habetur, ceteris omnibus rebus excellentius necesse est ametur, quoniam propter hanc amandum est quidquid aliud amatur.
passages.english: And if he should wish to die, not because he does not wish to live, but in order to live better after death, then he does not yet live as he wishes, but [will] when by dying he has reached what he wishes. But suppose he lives as he wishes, because he has forced and commanded himself not to wish what he cannot have, and to wish what he can, as Terence says: "Since what you wish cannot be done, wish what you can": is he blessed then, because he is patiently miserable? For the blessed life, if it is not loved, is not possessed. Further, if it is loved and possessed, it must be loved more excellently than all other things, since whatever else is loved must be loved for its sake.

passages.original: sicut aliis deinde nostrisque temporibus rara quidem, sed numquam ferme defuerunt; quae modum aliorum plurimum excederent. Plinius Secundus. doctissimus homo. quanto magis magisque praeterit saeculi excursus, minora corpora naturam ferre testatur; quod etiam Homerum commemorat saepe carmine fuisse conquestum, non haec uelut poetica figmenta deridens, sed in liistoricam fidem tamquam miraculorum naturalium scriptor adsumens. Verum, ut dixi, antiquorum magnitudines corporum inuenta plerumque ossa, quoniam diuturna sunt, etiam multo posterioribus saeculis produnt.
passages.english: just as in other later times and in our own there have been, rare indeed, but almost never lacking, [bodies] which greatly exceeded the measure of others. Pliny the Elder, a most learned man, testifies that the further the course of the age passes on, the smaller the bodies nature produces; and he records that Homer too often lamented this in his poetry, not mocking these things as poetic fictions, but accepting them as historical fact, as a writer on natural wonders. But, as I said, bones that are found, since they are long-lasting, often reveal the great size of the bodies of the ancients even to much later ages.
passages.notes: 'liistoricam' read as 'historicam' (scanning error). 'Plinius Secundus' is Pliny the Elder.

passages.original: Annorum autem numerositas cuiusque hominis, quae temporibus illis fuit, nullis nunc talibus documentis uenire in experimentum potest. Nec tamen ideo fides sacrae huic historiae deroganda est, cuius tanto inpudentius narrata non credimus, quanto inpleri certius praenuntiata conspicimus. Dicit tamen etiam idem Plinius esse adhuc gentem, ubi ducentos annos uiuitur. Si ergo humanarum uitarum diuturnitates, quas experti non sumus, hodie habere creduntur incognita nobis loca, quur non habuisse credantur et tempora?
passages.english: But the great number of years of each man's life in those times cannot now be put to the test by any such evidence. Yet trust in this sacred history must not on that account be withdrawn; the more surely we see its predictions being fulfilled, the more shameless it is for us not to believe its narrations. Yet the same Pliny says that there is still a people where men live two hundred years. If, then, places unknown to us are believed today to have lengths of human life which we have not experienced, why should times too not be believed to have had them?

passages.original: restat autem altera dedicatio uniuersae domus, cuius ipse Christus est fundamentum, quae differtur in finem, quando erit omnium resurrectio non moriturorum amplius. Siue autem domus Dei dicatur siue templum Dei siue ciuitas Dei, id ipsum est nec abhorret a Latini eloquii consuetudine. Nam et Vergilius imperiosissimam ciuitatem domum appellat Assaraci, Romanos uolens intellegi, qui de Assaraco per Troianos originem ducunt; et domum Aeneae eosdem ipsos, quia eo duce Troiani cum Italiam uenissent ab eis condita est Roma. Imitatus namque est poeta ille litteras sacras, in quibus dicitur domus Iacob iam ingens populus Hebraeorum.
passages.english: There remains, however, the other dedication, of the whole house, whose foundation is Christ himself; it is deferred until the end, when there will be the resurrection of all, who will die no more. Whether it is called the house of God, or the temple of God, or the city of God, it is the same thing, and it is not foreign to the usage of Latin speech. For Virgil too calls the most imperial city the house of Assaracus, meaning the Romans, who trace their origin from Assaracus through the Trojans; and he calls the same people the house of Aeneas, because Rome was founded by the Trojans when they had come to Italy under his leadership. For that poet imitated the sacred writings, in which the Hebrew people, already huge, is called the house of Jacob.

passages.original: aliam uero longe praestantiorem non de carnali, sed de spiritali semine, per quod pater est non unius gentis Israeliticae, sed omnium gentium, quae fidei eius uestigia consequuntur, quod promitti coepit his uerbis: Et benedicentur in te omnes tribus terrae. Hanc promissionem factam arbitratur Eusebius septuagensimo quinto anno aetatis Abrahae, tamquam mox ut facta est de Charra exierit Abraham; quoniam scripturae contradici non potest, ubi legitur: Abraham erat quinque et septuaginta annorum, cum exiit ex Charra.
passages.english: and the other, far more excellent, concerning not carnal but spiritual seed, through which he is father not of the one Israelite nation but of all nations that follow in the footsteps of his faith; this began to be promised in these words: "And in you all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed." Eusebius thinks this promise was made in the seventy-fifth year of Abraham's age, as though Abraham left Haran as soon as it was made, since scripture cannot be contradicted where we read: "Abraham was seventy-five years old when he went out from Haran."

passages.original: Unde et acerrime cernentibus aliquas occultas esse merito existimatur, exceptis eis sideribus, quae in alia parte orbis a nobis remotissima oriri et occidere perhibentur. Postremo quicumque uniuersum stellarum numerum conprehendisse et conscripsisse iactantur, sicut Aratus uel Eudoxus uel si qui alii sunt, eos libri huius contemnit auctoritas. Hic sane illa sententia ponitur, cuius apostolus meminit propter Dei gratiam commendandam: Credidit Abraham Deo, et deputatum est illi ad iustitiam; ne circumcisio gloriaretur gentesque incircumcisas ad fidem Christi nollet admitti. Hoc enim quando factum est, ut credenti Abrahae deputaretur fides ad iustitiam, nondum fuerat circumcisus.
passages.english: Hence it is rightly supposed that some are hidden even from those with the keenest sight, apart from those stars which are said to rise and set in another part of the world very far removed from us. Finally, whoever boast of having comprehended and written down the whole number of the stars, such as Aratus or Eudoxus or any others there may be, the authority of this book despises them. Here indeed is set that statement which the apostle recalls in order to commend the grace of God: "Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness"; so that the circumcision should not boast and refuse to admit the uncircumcised nations to the faith of Christ. For when this happened, that his faith was reckoned as righteousness to Abraham when he believed, he had not yet been circumcised.

passages.original: Ninus ergo iam secundus rex erat Assyriorum, qui patri suo Belo successerat, regni illius primo regi, quando in terra Chaldaeorum natus est Abraham. Erat etiam tempore illo regnum Sicyoniorum admodum paruum, a quo ille undecumque doctissimus Marcus Varro scribens de gente populi Romani, uelut antiquo tempore. exorsus est. Ab his enim Sicyoniorum regibus ad Athenienses peruenit, a quibus ad Latinos, inde Romanos. Sed ante conditam Romam in conparatione regni Assyriorum perexigua ista memorantur;
passages.english: So Ninus was already the second king of the Assyrians, having succeeded his father Belus, the first king of that kingdom, when Abraham was born in the land of the Chaldeans. At that time there was also the very small kingdom of the Sicyonians, from which that man most learned in every field, Marcus Varro, writing on the race of the Roman people, began, as from an ancient time. For from these kings of the Sicyonians he came to the Athenians, from them to the Latins, and thence to the Romans. But before the founding of Rome these things recorded are very slight in comparison with the kingdom of the Assyrians;

passages.original: Regnum autem Argiuorum simul cum Abrahae nepotibus ortum est, ubi primus regnauit Inachus. Sane, quod praetereundum non fuit, etiam aput sepulcrum septimi sui regis Thuriaci sacrificare Sicyonios solere Varro refert. Regnantibus porro octauis regibus, Armamitre Assyriorum, Sicyoniorum Leucippo et primo Argiuorum Inacho Deus locutus est ad Isaac adque ipsi quoque eadem, quae patri eius, duo illa promisit, semini scilicet eius terram Chanaan et in eius semine benedictionem cunctarum gentium.
passages.english: The kingdom of the Argives arose at the same time as Abraham's grandsons, and there Inachus reigned first. Indeed — something that ought not to be passed over — Varro reports that the Sicyonians were also accustomed to sacrifice at the tomb of their seventh king, Thuriacus. Further, when the eighth kings were reigning, Armamitres of the Assyrians, Leucippus of the Sicyonians, and Inachus, the first of the Argives, God spoke to Isaac and promised him too the same two things as to his father, namely the land of Canaan to his seed, and in his seed the blessing of all nations.

passages.original: Et constitutum est etiam de illo, ut, quisquis eum hominem fuisse dixisset, capitalem penderet poenam. Et quoniam fere in omnibus templis, ubi colebantur Isis et Serapis, erat etiam simulacrum, quod digito labiis inpresso admonere uideretur, ut silentium fieret: hoc significare idem Varro existimat, ut homines eos fuisse taceretur. Ille autem bos, quem mirabili uanitate decepta Aegyptus in eius honorem deliciis afluentibus alebat, quoniam eum sine sarcophago uiuum uenerabantur, Apis, non Serapis uocabatur.
passages.english: And it was also decreed concerning him that whoever said he had been a man should pay the capital penalty. And since in almost all the temples where Isis and Serapis were worshipped there was also an image which, with a finger pressed to its lips, seemed to warn that there should be silence, the same Varro thinks this signifies that it should be kept silent that they had been human beings. But that bull which Egypt, deceived by an astonishing vanity, fed in his honour with abundant delicacies, since they worshipped it living, without a sarcophagus, was called Apis, not Serapis.

passages.original: Et tamen Marcus Varro non uult fabulosis aduersus deos fidem adhibere figmentis, ne de maiestatis eorum dignitate indignum aliquid sentiat. Et ideo nec Areon pagon, ubi cum Atheniensibus Paulus apostolus disputauit, ex quo loco Areopagitae appellati sunt curiales urbis eiusdem, uult inde accepisse nomen, quod Mars, qui Graece Ἄρης dicitur, cum homicidii crimine reus fieret, iudicantibus duodecim dis in eo pago sex sententiis absolutus est (quia ubi paris numeri sententiae fuissent, praeponi absolutio damnationi solebat);
passages.english: And yet Marcus Varro does not want to lend credence to mythical fictions against the gods, lest he think anything unworthy of the dignity of their majesty. And for that reason he does not want the Areopagus, where the apostle Paul debated with the Athenians, and from which place the councillors of that same city were called Areopagites, to have received its name from the fact that Mars, who in Greek is called Ares, when he was put on trial on a charge of homicide, was acquitted on that hill by six votes, with twelve gods judging (because where the votes had been of an equal number, acquittal was customarily given precedence over condemnation);
passages.notes: Augustine treats pagus here as 'hill' (Greek pagos); in Latin pagus usually means 'district' or 'village', and the next sentence plays on the word.

passages.original: et tamen non fabulosam, sed historicam rationem de Athenarum uocabulo reddens tantam Neptuni et Mineruae litem suis litteris inserit, de cuius nomine potius illa ciuitas uocaretur, ut, cum prodigiorum ostentatione contenderent, inter eos iudicare nec Apollo consultus auderet, sed deorum iurgium finiendum, sicut memoratarum trium dearum ad Paridem Iuppiter, ita et iste ad homines mitteret, ubi uinceret Minerua suffragiis et in poena suarum suffragatricium uinceretur, quae in aduersariis suis uiris obtinere Athenas potuit, et amicas suas feminas Athenaeas habere non potuit. His temporibus, ut Varro scribit, regnante Atheniensibus Cranao, successore Cecropis, ut autem nostri Eusebius et Hieronymus, adhuc eodem Cecrope permanente, diluuium fuit, quod appellatum est Deucalionis, eo quod ipse regnabat in earum terrarum partibus, ubi maxime factum est. Hoc autem diluuium nequaquam ad Aegyptum adque ad eius uicina peruenit.
passages.english: and yet, giving not a mythical but a historical account of the name of Athens, he inserts into his writings so great a quarrel between Neptune and Minerva over which of them the city should rather be named after, that, when they contended by displaying portents, not even Apollo, when consulted, dared to judge between them; but just as Jupiter sent the three goddesses mentioned to Paris, so he too sent the dispute of the gods to be settled by human beings, where Minerva won by votes and was defeated in the punishment of the women who voted for her: she who could hold Athens against her adversaries the men could not have her friends the women called Athenians. In these times, as Varro writes, while Cranaus, Cecrops' successor, reigned over the Athenians, or, as our own Eusebius and Jerome say, while the same Cecrops still remained [king], there was the flood which was called Deucalion's, because he reigned in those parts of the lands where it chiefly occurred. But this flood by no means reached Egypt and its neighbouring regions.

passages.original: Responsum enim acceperant Peloponnenses tum demum se superaturos, si eorum regem non occidissent. Fefellit ergo eos habitu pauperis apparendo et in suam necem per iurgium prouocando. Unde ait Vergilius: Et iurgia Codri. Et hunc Athenienses tamquam deum sacrificiorum honore coluerunt. Quarto Latinorum rege Siluio Aeneae filio, non de Creusa, de qua fuit Ascanius, qui tertius ibi regnauit, sed de Lauinia Latini filia, quem postumum Aeneas dicitur habuisse, Assyriorum autem uicensimo et nono Oneo et Melantho Atheniensium sexto decimo, iudice autem Hebraeorum Heli sacerdote regnum Sicyoniorum consumtum est, quod per annos nongentos quinquaginta et nouem traditur fuisse porrectum.
passages.english: For the Peloponnesians had received an oracle that they would conquer only if they had not killed their king. So he deceived them by appearing in the dress of a poor man and provoking them to his own death by a quarrel. Hence Virgil says: "And the quarrels of Codrus." And the Athenians worshipped him as a god with the honour of sacrifices. When the fourth king of the Latins was Silvius, son of Aeneas, not by Creusa, mother of Ascanius who reigned there third, but by Lavinia daughter of Latinus, a son Aeneas is said to have had posthumously; when the twenty-ninth of the Assyrians was Oneus, and Melanthus the sixteenth of the Athenians; and when the priest Eli was judge of the Hebrews, the kingdom of the Sicyonians came to an end, which is said to have extended over nine hundred and fifty-nine years.
passages.notes: 'Oneo' as name of an Assyrian king is uncertain; I could not identify it.

passages.original: Eodem tempore nonnulli Sibyllam Erythraeam uaticinatam ferunt. Sibyllas autem Varro prodit plures fuisse, non unam. Haec sane Erythraea Sibylla quaedam de Christo manifesta conscripsit; quod etiam nos prius in Latina lingua uersibus male Latinis et non stantibus legimus per nescio cuius interpretis inperitiam, sicut post cognouimus. Nam uir clarissimus . Flaccianus, qui etiam proconsul fuit, homo facillimae facundiae multaeque doctrinae, cum de Christo conloqueremur, Graecum nobis codicem protulit, carmina esse dicens Sibyllae Erythraeae, ubi ostendit quodam loco in capitibus uersuum ordinem litterarum ita se habentem, ut haec in eo uerba legerentur: Ἰησοῦς Χρειστὸς Θεοῦ υἱὸς σωτήρ, quod est Latine, Iesus Christus Dei filius saluator.
passages.english: At the same time, some report that the Erythraean Sibyl prophesied. Varro, however, records that there were several Sibyls, not one. This Erythraean Sibyl certainly wrote some things about Christ that are plain; and we too first read this in the Latin language, in bad Latin verses that did not scan, through the incompetence of some translator or other, as we learned afterwards. For the most distinguished man Flaccianus, who was also proconsul, a man of the readiest eloquence and much learning, when we were talking together about Christ, brought out a Greek manuscript for us, saying that it was the poems of the Erythraean Sibyl, and in it he showed [us] in a certain place that the order of the letters at the heads of the lines was such that these words were read in it: Iēsous Chreistos Theou huios sōtēr, which in Latin is 'Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour'.
passages.notes: A stray period before 'Flaccianus' in the text has been ignored.

passages.original: Mortuum Romulum, cum et ipse non conparuisset, in deos, quod et uulgo notissimum est, rettulere Romani; quod usque adeo fieri iam desierat (nec postea nisi adulando, non errando, factum est temporibus Caesarum), ut Cicero magnis Romuli laudibus tribuat, quod non rudibus et indoctis temporibus, quando facile homines fallebantur, sed iam expolitis et eruditis meruerit hos honores, quamuis nondum efiferbuerat ac pullulauerat philosophorum subtilis et acuta loquacitas.
passages.english: When Romulus died, since he too had disappeared, the Romans enrolled him among the gods, as is very well known even to the common people; and this had by then so far ceased to be done (nor was it done afterwards except from flattery, not from error, in the times of the Caesars) that Cicero attributes it to Romulus' great praise that he earned these honours not in rude and unlearned times, when men were easily deceived, but in times already refined and educated, although the subtle and sharp loquacity of the philosophers had not yet boiled up and sprouted.
passages.notes: 'efiferbuerat' read as 'efferbuerat' (scanning error).

passages.original: Eo tempore Pittacus Mitylenaeus, alius e septem sapientibus, fuisse perhibetur. Et quinque ceteros, qui, ut septem numerentur, Thaleti, quem supra commemorauimus, et huic Pittaco adduntur, eo tempore fuisse scribit Eusebius, quo captiuus Dei populus in Babylonia tenebatur. Hi sunt autem: Solon Atheniensis, Chilon Lacedaemonius, Periandrus Corinthius, Cleobulus Lindius, Bias Prienaeus. Omnes hi, septem appellati sapientes, post poetas theologos claruerunt, quia genere uitae quodam laudabili praestabant hominibus ceteris et morum nonnulla praecepta sententiarum breuitate conplexi sunt.
passages.english: At that time Pittacus of Mytilene, another of the seven sages, is said to have lived. And Eusebius writes that the other five, who are added to Thales, whom we mentioned above, and to this Pittacus to make up the number seven, lived at the time when the captive people of God was held in Babylonia. They are: Solon of Athens, Chilon of Sparta, Periander of Corinth, Cleobulus of Lindos, Bias of Priene. All these, called the seven sages, became famous after the theological poets, because they surpassed other men by a certain praiseworthy manner of life and summed up some moral precepts in brief maxims.

passages.original: Tres prophetae de minoribus, Abdias, Naum, Ambacum, nec tempora sua dicunt ipsi, nec in chronicis Eusebii et Hieronymi, quando prophetauerint, inuenitur. Abdias enim positus est quidem ab eis cum Michaea, sed non eo loco, ubi notantur tempora, quando Michaeam prophetasse ex eius litteris constat; quod errore neglegenter describentium labores alienos existimo contigisse;
passages.english: Three of the minor prophets, Obadiah, Nahum and Habakkuk, neither state their own times themselves, nor is it found in the chronicles of Eusebius and Jerome when they prophesied. For Obadiah is indeed placed by them with Micah, but not in the place where the times are noted when Micah is established from his writings to have prophesied; which I think happened through the error of those who carelessly copy the labours of others;

passages.original: Frustra itaque uanissima praesumtione garriunt quidam dicentes, ex quo Aegyptus rationem siderum conprehendit, amplius quam centum annorum milia numerari. In quibus enim libris istum numerum collegerunt, qui non multum ante annorum duo milia litteras magistra Iside didicerunt? Non enim paruus auctor est in historia Varro, qui hoc prodidit, quod a litterarum etiam diuinarum ueritate non dissonat. Cum enim ab ipso primo homine, qui est appellatus Adam, nondum sex annorum milia conpleantur, quo modo non isti ridendi potius quam refellendi sunt, qui de spatio temporum tam diuersa et huic exploratae ueritati tam contraria persuadere conantur?
passages.english: So some people chatter in vain, with the emptiest presumption, saying that more than a hundred thousand years are counted since Egypt grasped the science of the stars. For in what books did they gather that number, who learned letters, with Isis as their teacher, not much more than two thousand years ago? For Varro, who reported this, is no small authority in history, and it does not disagree with the truth of the divine writings either. For since not yet six thousand years are completed from the first man himself, who was called Adam, how are these people not to be laughed at rather than refuted, who try to persuade [us] of things about the span of time so different and so contrary to this ascertained truth?

passages.original: Nonne aput Athenas et Epicurei clarebant, adserentes res humanas ad deorum curam non pertinere, et Stoici, qui contraria sentientes eas regi ti adque muniri dis adiutoribus et tutoribus disputabant? Unde miror quur Anaxagoras reus factus sit, quia solem dixit esse lapidem ardentem, negans utique deum, cum in eadem ciuitate gloria floruerit Epicurus uixeritque securus, non solum solem uel ullum siderum deum esse non credens, sed nec Iouem nec ullum deorum omnino in mundo habitare contendens, ad quem preces hominum supplicationesque perueniant.
passages.english: Were not both the Epicureans famous at Athens, asserting that human affairs are no concern of the gods, and the Stoics, who, holding the contrary view, argued that they are ruled and protected by the gods as helpers and guardians? Hence I wonder why Anaxagoras was put on trial because he said the sun was a burning stone, thereby denying it was a god, when in the same city Epicurus flourished in glory and lived secure, not only not believing that the sun or any of the stars was a god, but contending that neither Jupiter nor any of the gods at all dwells in the world, for the prayers and supplications of men to reach him.
passages.notes: 'regi ti' is evidently a scanning error; read 'regi'.

passages.original: Quod ut breuiter ostendam, inde oportet incipiam, quod ipse aduertit et posuit in libro memorato, quattuor esse quaedam, quae homines sine magistro, sine ullo doctrinae adminiculo, sine industria uel arte uiuendi, quae uirtus dicitur et procul dubio discitur, uelut naturaliter adpetunt, aut uoluptatem, qua delectabiliter mouetur corporis sensus, aut quietem, qua fit ut nullam molestiam corporis quisque patiatur, aut utramque, quam tamen uno nomine uoluptatis Epicurus appellat, aut uniuersaliter prima naturae, in quibus et haec sunt et alia, uel in corpore, ut membrorum integritas et salus adque incolumitas eius, uel in animo, ut sunt ea, quae uel parua uel magna in hominum reperiuntur ingeniis.
passages.english: To show this briefly, I must begin from what he himself observed and set down in the book mentioned: that there are four things which human beings seek as if by nature, without a teacher, without any aid of instruction, without the effort or art of living which is called virtue and which is beyond doubt learned.
