[They seek] either pleasure, by which the bodily sense is agreeably stirred; or repose, by which it comes about that one suffers no bodily discomfort; or both, which Epicurus nevertheless calls by the single name of pleasure; or, in general, the primary things of nature, among which are both these and others, whether in the body, such as soundness of the limbs and its health and safety, or in the mind, such as those [gifts], small or great, that are found in human natural capacities.

passages.original: Haec de Varronis libro, quantum potui, breuiter ac dilucide posui, sententias eius meis explicans uerbis. Quo modo autem refutatis ceteris unam eligat, quam uult esse Acaderaicorum ueterum (quos a Platone institutos usque ad Polemonem, qui ab illo quartus eius scholam tenuit, quae Academia dicta est, habuisse certa dogmata uult uideri et ob hoc distinguit ab Academicis nonis, quibus incerta sunt omnia, quod philosophiae genus ab Arcesila coepit successore Polemonis), eamque sectam, id est ueterum Academicorum, sicut dubitatione ita omni errore carere arbitretur, longum est per omnia demonstrare;
passages.english: These things from Varro's book I have set out, as far as I could, briefly and clearly, explaining his views in my own words. But how, having refuted the rest, he chooses one, which he holds to be that of the Old Academics (whom, founded by Plato and continuing down to Polemo, who was fourth after him to hold his school, which was called the Academy, he wants to be seen as having had certain doctrines, and for this reason he distinguishes them from the New Academics, for whom everything is uncertain, a kind of philosophy that began with Arcesilaus, the successor of Polemo), and how he judges that this sect, that is, of the Old Academics, is as free from all error as it is from doubt, would be a long matter to demonstrate in every detail;
passages.notes: 'Acaderaicorum' and 'nonis' are scanning errors for Academicorum and nouis (New).

passages.original: Nihil quippe aliud in eis quaeritur quam fines bonorum et malorum. Inuentis autem bonorum finibus profecto e contrario sunt malorum. Hae autem ut fiant duodecim sectae, illa quattuor triplicantur, uoluptas, quies, utrumque et prima naturae, quae primigenia Varro uocat. Haec quippe quattuor dum singillatim uirtuti aliquando subduntur, ut non propter se ipsa, sed propter officium uirtutis adpetenda uideantur, aliquando praeferuntur, ut non propter se ipsa, sed propter haec adipiscenda uel conseruanda necessaria uirtus putetur, aliquando iunguntur, ut propter se ipsa et uirtus et ista adpetenda credantur, quaternarium numerum triplum reddunt et ad duodecim sectas perueniunt.
passages.english: For nothing else is sought in them than the ends of goods and of evils. And when the ends of goods are found, those of evils are certainly the contrary. Now, so that there come to be twelve sects, those four are tripled: pleasure, rest, both together, and the primary things of nature, which Varro calls primigenia. For these four, while taken one by one they are sometimes subordinated to virtue, so that they seem to be desired not for their own sake but for the sake of virtue's duty; sometimes preferred [to it], so that virtue is thought necessary not for its own sake but for obtaining or preserving these; sometimes joined [with it], so that both virtue and these are believed desirable for their own sake: [thus] they make the number four threefold and arrive at twelve sects.

passages.original: De bonorum autem et e contrario malorum finibus negant ullo modo esse dubitandum et hanc inter se et nouos Academicos adfirmant esse distantiam, nec eorum interest quidquam, siue Cynico siue alio quolibet habitu et uictu in his finibus, quos ueros putant, quisque philosophetur. Ex tribus porro illis uitae generibus, otioso, actuoso et quod ex utroque conpositum est, hoc tertium sibi placere adseuerant. Haec sensisse adque docuisse Academicos ueteres Varro adserit, auctore Antiocho, magistro Ciceronis et suo, quem sane Cicero in pluribus fuisse Stoicum quam ueterem Academicum I unIt uideri. Sed quid ad nos, qui potius de rebus ipsis iudicare debemus, quam pro magno de hominibus quid quisque senserit scire?
passages.english: But concerning the ends of goods, and conversely of evils, they deny that there should be any doubt at all, and they affirm that this is the difference between themselves and the New Academics; nor does it matter to them at all whether anyone practises philosophy in the Cynic dress and way of life or in any other, within these ends which they think true. Further, of those three kinds of life, the leisured, the active, and that which is compounded of both, they assert that this third pleases them. Varro asserts that the Old Academics held and taught these things, on the authority of Antiochus, the teacher of Cicero and of himself, whom Cicero indeed makes appear to have been in more respects a Stoic than an Old Academic. But what is that to us, who ought rather to judge about the things themselves than to know, as a great matter, what each person thought about them?
passages.notes: 'I unIt uideri' is corrupt; probably 'facit uideri' ('makes appear'), translated so.

passages.original: Ipse est Deus, cuius diuinus Spiritus per eos locutus est, quorum praedicta adque conpleta per ecclesiam, quam uidemus toto orbe diffusam, in libris superioribus posui. Ipse est Deus, quem Varro doctissimus Romanorum Iouem putat, quamuis nesciens quid loquatur; quod tamen ideo commemorandum putaui, quoniam uir tantae scientiae nec nullum istum Deum potuit existimare nec uilem. Hunc enim eum esse credidit, quem summum putauit deum. Postremo ipse est Deus, quem doctissimus philosophorum, quamuis Christianorum acerrimus inimicus, etiam per eorum oracula, quos deos putat, deum magnum Porphyrius confitetur.
passages.english: He is the God whose divine Spirit spoke through those men whose predictions, and their fulfilment through the Church which we see spread through the whole world, I set out in the earlier books. He is the God whom Varro, the most learned of the Romans, thinks to be Jupiter, though not knowing what he says; yet I thought this worth mentioning because a man of such knowledge could think this God neither nonexistent nor contemptible. For he believed him to be the one whom he thought the supreme god. Finally, he is the God whom Porphyry, the most learned of the philosophers, though the fiercest enemy of the Christians, acknowledges as the great God, even through the oracles of those whom he thinks gods.

passages.original: Quae Porphyrius dicat oraculis deorum responsa esse de Christo.
passages.english: What Porphyry says was given in reply by the oracles of the gods concerning Christ.
passages.notes: A chapter heading.

passages.original: Item ad ea, quae interrogauit Apollinem, quid melius, uerbum siue ratio an lex: cRespondit, inquit, uersibus haec dicens.\' Ac deinde subicit Apollinis uersus, in quibus et isti sunt, ut quantum satis est inde decerpam: (In Deum uero, inquit, generatorem et in regem ante omnia, quem tremit et caelum et terra adque mare et infernorum abdita et ipsa numina perhorrescunt; quorum lex est Pater, quem ualde sancti honorant Hebraei.) Tali oraculo dei sui Apollinis Porphyrius tam magnum Deum dixit Hebraeorum, ut eum et ipsa numina perhorrescant. Cum ergo Deus iste dixerit: Sacrificans dis eradicabitur, miror quod ipse Porphyrius non perhorruerit et sacrificans dis eradicari non formidauerit.
passages.english: Likewise, regarding what he asked Apollo, which is better, the word (or reason) or the law, 'He replied,' he says, 'saying this in verse.' And then he adds Apollo's verses, among which are also these, so that I may excerpt from them as much as suffices: 'In God indeed,' he says, 'the begetter and king before all things, at whom heaven and earth and sea and the hidden places of the underworld tremble, and before whom the divine powers themselves shudder; whose law is the Father, whom the very holy Hebrews greatly honour.' By such an oracle of his god Apollo, Porphyry declared the God of the Hebrews so great that even the divine powers themselves shudder before him. Since, then, this God has said, 'He who sacrifices to the gods shall be rooted out,' I wonder that Porphyry himself did not shudder and did not fear to be rooted out for sacrificing to the gods.
passages.notes: The oracle's opening 'In God...' appears grammatically incomplete in the excerpt. Stray 'c' before 'Respondit' omitted.

passages.original: Sane Christum laudans uel Porphyrius uel Hecate, cum dicat eum ipsum fataliter dedisse Christianis, ut inplicarentur errore, causas tamen eiusdem, sicut putat, pandit erroris. Quas antequam ex uerbis eius exponam, prius quaero, si fataliter dedit Christus Christianis erroris inplicationem, utrum nolens an nolens dederit.
passages.english: Certainly, whether it is Porphyry or Hecate who praises Christ, when saying that he himself fatefully granted to the Christians that they should be entangled in error, [the speaker] nevertheless lays open the causes, as he thinks, of that same error. Before I set these out from his words, I first ask: if Christ fatefully gave the Christians entanglement in error, did he give it willingly or unwillingly?
passages.notes: Text reads 'nolens an nolens'; evidently 'uolens an nolens' (willingly or unwillingly), as the following context confirms.

passages.original: Hebraeorum opinionem dicit Hieronymus), iudicium nouissimum prophetat dicens: Ecce uenit, dicit Dominus omnipotens; et quis sustinebit diem introitus -eius, aut quis ferre poterit ut adspiciat eum? Quia ipse ingreditur quasi ignis conflatorii et quasi herba lauantium; et sedebit conflans et emundans sicut argentum et sicut aurum, et emundabit filios Leui, et fundet eos sicut aurum et argentum; et erunt Domino offerentes hostias in iustitia, et placebit Domino sacrificium Iudae et Hierusalem, sicut diebus pristinis et sicut annis prioribus.
passages.english: ...Jerome says is the opinion of the Hebrews), prophesies the last judgement, saying: 'Behold, he comes, says the Lord Almighty; and who will endure the day of his coming, or who will be able to bear to look upon him? For he comes in like the fire of a smelting furnace and like the fullers' herb; and he will sit smelting and purifying as silver and as gold, and he will purify the sons of Levi and pour them out like gold and silver; and they will be offering sacrifices to the Lord in righteousness, and the sacrifice of Judah and Jerusalem will please the Lord, as in the former days and as in earlier years.'
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; the subject (the prophet, presumably Malachi) is lost.

passages.original: Cum uero illa, quae magis dolere potest, non possit mori, quid momenti adfert quur illa corpora, quoniam futura sunt in doloribus, ideo etiam moritura esse credamus? Dixerunt quidem Platonici ex terrenis corporibus moribundisque membris esse animae et metuere et cupere et dolere adque gaudere; unde Vergilius: lHinc, inquit, (id est ex moribundis terreni corporis membris) metuunt cupiuntque, dolent gaudentque.\' Sed conuicimus eos in duodecimo huius operis libro, habere animas secundum ipsos ab omni etiam corporis labe purgatas diram cupiditatem.
passages.english: But since that which is more able to feel pain, [the soul,] cannot die, what weight does it carry that we should believe those bodies, because they will be in pain, will therefore also be subject to death? The Platonists did indeed say that the soul's fearing and desiring and grieving and rejoicing come from earthly bodies and dying limbs; whence Virgil says: 'From this' (that is, from the dying limbs of the earthly body) 'they fear and desire, grieve and rejoice.' But we have convicted them, in the twelfth book of this work, of holding that souls, even when purged according to them of every stain of the body, have a dire desire
passages.notes: The sentence continues into the following context. Stray 'l' before 'Hinc' omitted.

passages.original: Est in Marci Varronis libris, quorum inscriptio est: De gente populi Romani, quod eisdem uerbis, quibus ibi legitur, et hic ponam: \'In caelo, inquit, mirabile exstitit portentum: nam stellam Veneris nobilissimam, quam Plautus Vesperugiuem, Homerus Hesperon appellat, pulcherrimam dicens, Castor scribit tantum portentum exstitisse, ut mutaret colorem, magnitudinem, figuram, cursum; quod factum ita neque antea nec postea sit. Hoc factum Ogygo rege dicebant Adrastos Cyzicenos et Dion Neapolites, mathematici nobiles.\' Hoc certe Varro tantus auctor portentum non appellaret, nisi esse contra naturam uideretur.
passages.english: There is in the books of Marcus Varro entitled 'On the Race of the Roman People' something that I shall set down here in the very words in which it is read there: 'In the sky,' he says, 'a marvellous portent appeared: for Castor writes that in the most renowned star of Venus, which Plautus calls Vesperugo and Homer Hesperus, calling it most beautiful, so great a portent appeared that it changed its colour, size, shape and course; which had never happened thus either before or since. Adrastus of Cyzicus and Dion of Naples, noted astronomers, said this happened in the reign of King Ogygus.' Certainly Varro, so great an authority, would not have called this a portent unless it seemed to be contrary to nature.
passages.notes: 'Vesperugiuem' is a scanning error for Vesperuginem. 'Adrastos Cyzicenos' and 'Dion Neapolites' are not otherwise identified.

passages.original: Nos autem in diuinis libris legimus etiam solem ipsum et stetisse, cum hoc a Domino Deo petiuisset uir sanctus Iesus Naue, donec coeptum proelium uictoria terminaret, et retrorsum redisse, ut regi Ezechiae quindecim anni ad uiuendum additi hoc etiam prodigio promissioni Dei significarentur adiuncto. Sed ista quoque miracula, quae meritis sunt concessa sanctorum, quando credunt isti facta, magicis artibus tribuunt. Unde illud est, quod superius commemoraui dixisse Vergilium: Sistere aquam fluuiis et uertere sidera retro. Nam et fluuium stetisse superius inferiusque fluxisse, cum populus Dei ductore supra memorato Iesu Naue uiam carperet, et Helia propheta transeunte ac postea discipulo eius Helisaeo id esse factum in sacris litteris legimus, et retro uersum fuisse maximum sidus regnante Ezechia modo commemorauimus. Quod uero de Lucifero Varro scripsit, non est illic dictum alicui petenti homini id fuisse concessum.
passages.english: But we read in the divine books that even the sun itself both stood still, when the holy man Joshua son of Nun had asked this of the Lord God, until he could end the battle he had begun with victory, and went backwards, so that the fifteen years added to King Hezekiah's life might be signified by this portent too, joined to God's promise. But these miracles also, which were granted to the merits of the saints, when these people believe they happened, they attribute to magic arts. Hence that line which I mentioned above that Virgil said: 'To halt the water in the rivers and turn the stars backward.' For we read in the sacred writings both that a river stood still above and flowed on below, when the people of God were making their way under the aforementioned leader Joshua son of Nun, and that this was done when the prophet Elijah crossed, and afterwards his disciple Elisha; and we have just mentioned that the greatest star turned back in the reign of Hezekiah. But as for what Varro wrote about Lucifer, it is not said there that this was granted to any man who asked for it.
passages.notes: Lucifer = the morning star (Venus).

passages.original: Est itaque quidam uitae modus nec tam malae, ut his qui eam uiuunt nihil prosit ad capessendum regnum caelorum largitas elemosynarum, quibus etiam iustorum sustentatur inopia et fiunt amici qui in tabernacula aeterna suscipiant, nec tam bonae, ut ad tantam beatitudinem adipiscendam eis ipsa sufficiat, nisi eorum meritis, quos amicos fecerint, misericordiam consequantur. (Mirari autem soleo etiam aput Vergilium reperiri istam Domini sententiam, ubi ait: Facite uobis amicos de mammona iniquitatis, ut et ipsi recipiant uos in tabernacula aeterna; cui est et illa simillima: Qui recipit prophetam in nomine prophetae, mercedem prophetae accipiet; et qui recipit iustum in nomine iusti, mercedem iusti accipiet.
passages.english: There is, therefore, a certain manner of life neither so bad that generosity in almsgiving is of no use to those who live it for gaining the kingdom of heaven (alms by which even the need of the righteous is relieved and friends are made who may receive [them] into the eternal dwellings), nor so good that it suffices of itself for attaining so great a blessedness, unless they obtain mercy through the merits of those whom they have made friends. (I am often amazed, too, that this saying of the Lord is found even in Virgil, where [the Lord] says: 'Make for yourselves friends by means of the mammon of unrighteousness, so that they also may receive you into the eternal dwellings'; to which this also is very similar: 'He who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet's reward; and he who receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man will receive a righteous man's reward.'
passages.notes: The parenthesis continues beyond the passage.

passages.original: -eius regnum sempiternum: et alia quae ad hoc pertinentia in libro uicensimo posui, siue quae non posui et tamen in eisdem litteris scripta sunt, uenient et haec, sicut ista uenerunt, quae increduli nOli putabant esse uentura. Idem quippe Deus utraque promisit, utraque uentura esse praedixit. quem perhorrescunt numina paganorum, etiam teste Porphyrio, nobilissimo philosopho paganorum.
passages.english: ...'his kingdom is everlasting'; and the other things pertaining to this which I set out in the twentieth book, or which I did not set out and yet are written in the same scriptures, these too will come, just as those have come which unbelievers thought would not come. For the same God promised both, foretold that both would come, before whom the divine powers of the pagans shudder, as even Porphyry, the most renowned philosopher of the pagans, testifies.
passages.notes: 'nOli' is a scanning error for 'non'.

passages.original: Romuli autem aetatem minus his sescentis annis iam inueteratis litteris adque doctrinis omnique illo antiquo ex inculta hominum uita errore sublato fuisse cernimus.\' Et paulo post de eodem Romulo ita loquitur, quod ad hunc pertinet sensum: \'Ex quointellegi potest, inquit, permultis annis ante Homerum fuisse quam Romulum. ut iam doctis hominibus ac temporibus ipsis eruditis ad fingendum uix quicquam esset loci. Antiquitas enim recipit fabulas, fictas etiam nonnumquam incondite; haec aetas autem iam exculta, praesertim eludens omne quodfieri non potest, respuit.\' Unus e numero doctissimorum hominum idemque eloquentissimus omnium Marcus Tullius Cicero propterea dicit diuinitatem Romuli mirabiliter creditam. quod erudita iam tempora fuerunt, quae falsitatem non reciperent fabularum. Quis autem Romulum deum nisi Roma credidit, adque id parua et incipiens? Tum deinde posteris seruare fuerat necesse quod acceperant a maioribus, ut cum ista superstitione in lacte quodam modo matris ebibita cresceret ciuitas adque ad tam magnum perueniret imperium, ut ex eius fastigio, uelut ex altiore quodam loco, alias quoque gentes, quibus dominaretur, hac sua opinione perfunderet, ut non quidem crederent, sed tamen dicerent deum Romulum, ne ciuitatem, cui seruiebant, de conditore eius offenderent.
passages.english: But we see that the age of Romulus was less than six hundred years ago, when letters and learning had already grown old, and all that ancient error arising from the uncultivated life of men had been removed.' And a little later he speaks of the same Romulus in words to this effect: 'From this it can be understood,' he says, 'that Homer lived very many years before Romulus, so that, men being already learned and the times themselves educated, there was scarcely any room left for invention. For antiquity accepted fables, sometimes even crudely invented; but this age, already cultivated, especially as it mocks everything that cannot happen, rejects [them].' One of the number of the most learned men, and at the same time the most eloquent of all, Marcus Tullius Cicero, says that the divinity of Romulus was wonderfully believed for this reason: that the times were already learned, times which would not accept the falsehood of fables. But who believed Romulus a god except Rome, and that when it was small and just beginning? Then afterwards the descendants had to preserve what they had received from their ancestors, so that the city grew with this superstition drunk in, as it were, with its mother's milk, and came to so great an empire that from its summit, as from some higher place, it poured this opinion of its own over other nations too, which it ruled, so that they did not indeed believe, but nevertheless said, that Romulus was a god, lest they offend the city they served regarding its founder,
passages.notes: 'quointellegi' and 'quodfieri' read as 'quo intellegi' and 'quod fieri'. The final sentence continues into the following passage.

passages.original: ciuitatibus autem mors ipsa poena est, quae uidetur a poena singulos uindicare. Debet enim constituta sic esse ciuitas, ut aeterna sit. Itaque nullus interitus est rei publicae naturalis, ut hominis, in quo mors non modo necessaria est, uerum etiam optanda persaepe. Ciuitas autem cum tollitur, deletur, exstinguitur: simile est quodam modo, ut parua magnis conferamus, ac si omnis hic mundus intereat et concidat.\' Hoc ideo dixit Cicero, quia mundum non interiturum cum Platonicis sentit. Constat ergo eum pro ea salute uoluisse bellum suscipi a ciuitate, qua fit ut maneat hic ciuitas, sicut dicit, aeterna, quamuis morientibus et nascentibus singulis.
passages.english: but for cities death itself is a punishment, though it seems to free individuals from punishment. For a city ought to be so constituted as to be eternal. Thus there is no natural end for a commonwealth, as there is for a man, for whom death is not only necessary but very often even desirable. But when a city is removed, it is destroyed, it is extinguished: it is in a way similar, to compare small things with great, as if this whole world were to perish and collapse.' Cicero said this because he holds with the Platonists that the world will not perish. It is clear, then, that he wanted war to be undertaken by a city for that safety by which the city remains here, as he says, eternal, although individuals die and are born,
passages.notes: Begins and ends mid-sentence.

passages.original: sicut medici dicunt, nullis medicamentis sanabilem. Aut ergo praecidi solet et a corpore separari membrum ubi nascitur, aut, ut aliquanto diutius homo uiuat, tamen inde morte quamlibet tardius adfutura, secundum Hippocratis ut ferunt sententiam omnis est omittenda curatio. Hoc illa a perito medico et suae domui familiarissimo acceperat et ad solum Deum se orando conuerterat. Admonetur in somnis propinquante Pascha, ut in parte feminarum obseruanti ad baptisterium, quaecumque illi baptizata primitus occurrisset.
passages.english: which, as doctors say, is curable by no medicines. So either the member where it arises is usually cut off and separated from the body, or, so that the person may live somewhat longer, though death will come from it however late, all treatment should be omitted, according to the opinion, as they say, of Hippocrates. She had received this [advice] from a skilled doctor very intimate with her household, and had turned to God alone in prayer. She is advised in a dream, as Easter approached, that in the women's section at the baptistery she should watch for whatever woman newly baptized first met her,
passages.notes: Begins mid-sentence ('a cancer ... a thing which'). 'obseruanti' is presumably for 'obseruaret' or similar; sense is that she should watch for. Sentence continues: '[and ask her to] make the sign of Christ on the place'.

passages.original: Iam uero contra illud, quod dixi superius, etiam istum considerantes adque tractantes elementorum ordinem, quo confidunt, non inueniunt omnino quod dicant. Sic est enim hinc sursum uersus terra prima, aqua secunda, tertius aer, quartum caelum, ut super omnia sit animae natura. Nam et Aristoteles quintum corpus eam dixit esse et Plato nullum.
passages.english: Now, against what I said above, even when they consider and examine this order of the elements in which they trust, they find nothing at all to say. For it is thus, from here upwards: earth first, water second, air third, the heaven fourth, so that above all is the nature of the soul. For Aristotle said it was a fifth body, and Plato that it was no body.
passages.notes: 'Plato nullum' understood as 'no body at all'.

passages.original: Iam si ad eorum miracula ueniamus, quae facta a dis suis obponunt martyribus nostris, nonne etiam ipsa pro nobis facere et nobis reperientur omnino proficere? Nam inter magna miracula deorum suorum profecto magnum illud est, quod Varro commemorat, Vestalem uirginem, cum periclitaretur falsa suspicione de stupro, cribrum inplesse aqua de Tiberi et ad suos iudices nulla eius parte stillante portasse. Quis aquae pondus supra cribrum tenuit?
passages.english: Now if we come to their miracles, which they set against our martyrs as done by their gods, will not even these be found to act on our behalf and to benefit us altogether? For among the great miracles of their gods, surely that one is great which Varro records: that a Vestal virgin, when she was in danger through a false suspicion of unchastity, filled a sieve with water from the Tiber and carried it to her judges with no part of it dripping. Who held the weight of the water on the sieve?

passages.original: Quur denique aer est medius inter summa caeli et nuda terrarum, quaqua uersum orbis extenditur, si locus eius inter caelum et aquas, sicut aquarum inter ipsum et terras est constitutus? Postremo si ita est elementorum ordo dispositus, ut secundum Platonem duobus mediis, id est aere et aqua, duo extrema, id est ignis et terra, iungantur caelique obtineat ille summi locum, haec autem imi uelut fundaminis mundi. et ideo in caelo esse non potest terra: quur est ipse ignis in terra?
passages.english: Why, finally, is air in the middle between the heights of heaven and the bare lands, wherever the globe extends, if its place has been set between heaven and the waters, as that of the waters is between it and the lands? Lastly, if the order of the elements is so arranged that, according to Plato, the two extremes, that is fire and earth, are joined by two means, that is air and water, and the former holds the place of the highest heaven, while the latter [holds that] of the lowest, as the foundation of the world, and therefore earth cannot be in heaven: why is fire itself on earth?

passages.original: In carnem quippe conuersa est eius, qui talibus uixit alimentis, et ea, quae macies ostenderat, detrimenta subpleuit. Utrum ergo illi redeat homini cuius caro prius fuit, an illi potius cuius postea facta est, ad hoc percontantur, ut fidem resurrectionis inludant ac sic animae humanae aut alternantes, sicut Plato, ueras infelicitates falsasque promittant beatitudines aut post multas itidem per diuersa corpora reuolutiones aliquando tamen eam, sicut Porphyrius, finire miserias et ad eas numquam redire fateantur; non tamen corpus habendo inmortale, sed corpus omne fugiendo.
passages.english: For it has been converted into the flesh of the one who lived on such food, and has made good the losses which his emaciation had shown. So whether it will return to the man whose flesh it was first, or rather to the one whose flesh it became afterwards — this they ask in order to mock faith in the resurrection, and so either promise the human soul, as Plato does, alternating true unhappinesses and false beatitudes, or else admit, as Porphyry does, that after many revolutions likewise through various bodies it does at some time end its miseries and never returns to them; yet not by having an immortal body, but by fleeing every body.

passages.original: et ad hoc meliores quosque in his malis adiuuat gratia, ut quanto fideliore, tanto fortiore corde tolerentur. Ad quam rem etiam philosophiam prodesse dicunt docti huius saeculi, quam di quibusdam paucis, ait Tullius, ueram dederunt; nec hominibus, inquit, ab his aut datum est donum maius aut potuit ullum dari: usque adeo et ipsi, contra quos agimus, quoquo modo conpulsi sunt in habenda non quacumque, sed uera philosophia diuinam gratiam confiteri.
passages.english: and to this end grace helps all the better people in these evils, that they may be endured with a heart the stronger as it is the more faithful. For this purpose the learned of this world say that philosophy too is of use — philosophy which the gods, Tullius says, have given in its true form to a certain few; and no greater gift, he says, has been given to men by them, or could be given: so far have even those against whom we argue been compelled, in one way or another, to confess divine grace in the possession not of just any philosophy, but of true philosophy.
passages.notes: Begins mid-sentence.

passages.original: Quo modo Porphyrii definitio, qua beatis animis putat corpus omne fugiendum, ipsius Platonis sententia destruatur, qui dicit summum Deum dis promisisse, ut numquam corporibus exuerentur.
passages.english: How the definition of Porphyry, by which he thinks that every body must be fled by blessed souls, is destroyed by the opinion of Plato himself, who says that the supreme God promised the gods that they would never be stripped of their bodies.
passages.notes: Chapter heading.

passages.original: Sed Porphyrius ait, inquiunt, ut beata sit anima, corpus esse omne fugiendum. Nihil ergo prodest, quia incorruptibile diximus futurum corpus, si anima beata non erit, nisi omne corpus effugerit. Sed iam et hinc in libro memorato quantum oportuit disputaui;
passages.english: 'But Porphyry says,' they say, 'that for the soul to be blessed, every body must be fled.' So it is of no use that we have said the body will be incorruptible, if the soul will not be blessed unless it escapes every body. But I have already argued about this in the book mentioned, as much as was needed;

passages.original: quoniam est inpossibilis, ideo resurrectionem carnis non esse credendam. Apertissime quippe iuxta eundem philosophum. ubi dis a se factis promisit Deus non factus inmortalitatem, quod inpossibile est se dixit esse facturum. Sic enim eum locutum narrat Plato: \'Quoniam estis orti, inquit, inmortales esse et indissolubiles non potestis; non tamen dissoluemini neque uos ulla mortis fata periment nec erunt ualentiora quam consilium meum, quod maius est uinculum ad perpetuitatem uestram quam illa (quibus estis conligati.\' Si non solum absurdi, sed surdi non sunt qui haec audiunt non utique dubitant dis factis ab illo Deo qui eos fecit secundum Platonem quod est inpossibile fuisse promissum.
passages.english: that, since it is impossible, the resurrection of the flesh is therefore not to be believed. For most plainly, according to the same philosopher, when the unmade God promised immortality to the gods he had made, he said that he would do what is impossible. For Plato reports that he spoke thus: 'Since you have come into being,' he says, 'you cannot be immortal and indissoluble; yet you will not be dissolved, nor will any fates of death destroy you, nor will they be stronger than my purpose, which is a greater bond for your perpetuity than those by which you are bound together.' If those who hear this are not only not absurd but not deaf, they surely do not doubt that what is impossible was promised to the gods made by that God who, according to Plato, made them.
passages.notes: Begins mid-sentence. Wordplay absurdi/surdi. Stray parenthesis before 'quibus' omitted.

passages.original: Non ergo, ut beatae pint animae, corpus est omne fugiendum, sed corpus incorruptibile recipiendum. Et in quo conuenientius incorruptibili corpore laetabuntur, quam in quo corruptibili gemuerunt? Sic enim non in eis erit illa dira cupiditas, quam posuit ex Platone Vergilius, ubi ait:
passages.english: So, in order that souls may be blessed, it is not every body that must be fled, but an incorruptible body that must be received. And in what [body] will they more fittingly rejoice, once it is incorruptible, than in that in which, while it was corruptible, they groaned? For thus that dreadful desire will not be in them which Virgil set down, drawing on Plato, where he says:
passages.notes: "pint" is a scanning error for "sint" ("may be"). The passage ends with the introduction to a quotation from Virgil that is not included.

passages.original: ut non singuli haec singula, sed ambo et singuli utrumque dicerent: puto quod uiderent esse iam consequens, ut et redirent animae ad corpora et talia reciperent corpora, in quibus beate adque inmortaliter uiuerent. Quoniam secundum Platonem etiam sanctae animae ad humana corpora redibunt; secundum Porphyrium ad mala mundi huius sanctae animae non redibunt: dicat itaque cum Platone Porphyrius: \'Redibunt ad corpora\'; dicat Plato cum Porphyrio: \'Non redibunt ad mala\': et ad ea corpora redire consentient, in quibus nulla patiantur mala. Haec itaque non erunt nisi illa quae promittit Deus, beatas animas in aeternum cum sua aeterna carne facturus.
passages.english: so that it was not each of them saying his own one thing, but both of them, and each, saying both things, I think they would see that it now follows both that souls return to bodies and that they receive such bodies as those in which they might live blessedly and immortally. For according to Plato even holy souls will return to human bodies; according to Porphyry holy souls will not return to the evils of this world. So let Porphyry say with Plato, 'They will return to bodies'; let Plato say with Porphyry, 'They will not return to evils'; and they will agree that [souls] return to those bodies in which they suffer no evils. And these will be none other than those which God promises, who is going to make souls blessed for eternity together with their own eternal flesh.
passages.notes: The opening clause continues a sentence begun in the preceding context ("if Plato had granted to Porphyry... if Porphyry had granted to Plato...").

passages.original: Nonnulli nostri propter quoddam praeclarissimum loquendi genus et propter nonnulla, quae ueraciter sensit, amantes Platonem dicunt eum aliquid simile nobis etiam de mortuorum resurrectione sensisse. Quod quidem sic tangit in libris de re publica Tullius, ut eum lusisse potius, quam quod id uerum esset, adfirmet dicere uoluisse.
passages.english: Some of our own people, who love Plato for a certain most splendid manner of speaking and for some things which he truly perceived, say that he held something similar to us even about the resurrection of the dead. Cicero touches on this in his books On the Republic in such a way that he asserts that [Plato] was playing rather than meaning to say it because it was true.

passages.original: Quapropter Plato et Porphyrius, uel potius quicumque illos diligunt et adhuc uiuunt, si nobis consentiunt etiam sanctas animas ad corpora redituras, sicut ait Plato, nec tamen ad mala ulla redituras, sicut ait Porphyrius, ut ex his fiat consequens, quod fides praedicat Christiana, talia corpora recepturas, in quibus sine ullo malo in aeternum feliciter uiuant, adsumant etiam hoc de Varrone, ut ad eadem corpora redeant, in quibus antea fuerunt, et aput eos tota quaestio de carnis in aeternum resurrectione soluetur.
passages.english: Therefore, if Plato and Porphyry, or rather whoever love them and are still living, agree with us that holy souls too will return to bodies, as Plato says, and yet will not return to any evils, as Porphyry says, so that from these [two positions] it follows, as the Christian faith proclaims, that they will receive such bodies as those in which they may live happily for eternity without any evil, let them also take this from Varro: that they return to the same bodies in which they were before; and then, among them, the whole question of the resurrection of the flesh for eternity will be resolved.

passages.original: Nam secundum interpretes septuaginta ista sunt ad Giezi uerba prophetae: Nonne cor meum iit tecum, quando conuersus est uir de curru suo in obuiam tibi et accepisti pecuniam? et cetera; sicut autem ex Hebraeo interpretatus est presbyter Hieronymus: Nonne cor meum, inquit, in prae senti erat, quando reuersus est homo de curru suo in occursum tui? Corde suo ergo se dixit hoc uidisse propheta, adiuto quidem mirabiliter nullo dubitante diuinitus.
passages.english: For according to the Septuagint translators these are the prophet's words to Gehazi: 'Did not my heart go with you, when the man turned from his chariot to meet you and you took the money?' and so on; but as the priest Jerome translated from the Hebrew: 'Was not my heart,' he says, 'present, when the man turned back from his chariot to meet you?' So the prophet said that he saw this with his heart, aided, no one doubts, in a wonderful way by God.
passages.notes: "prae senti" is a scanning split for "praesenti" ("present").
